blocks.h: WAITING FOR MY BIRD
Roya Publication No. 106
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Every morning at first light, Nasim Nazari climbs to the roof of his house in Maidan Shahr, an hour west of Kabul, and lets his pigeons go. He fixes radios and telephones in the bazaar. He has a wife who sews dresses and makes up proverbs, and a daughter of eight who will not take off her pink sandals. High above the town there is a thin, patient buzzing that never goes away. Nasim believes it is looking for somebody else.

Seven and a half thousand miles away, in a cold metal trailer in the Nevada desert, Kayla Rourke works the night shift. She is a sensor operator. She points the camera of an unmanned Reaper drone, and when the order comes, she holds the laser. She has been watching a house in Wardak for forty-one days. She knows the mulberry tree, the blue door that sticks, and the man who goes up to the roof every dawn and looks straight at the sky.
She has written it down, in block capitals, so nobody can misread it: possible awareness of surveillance.

The book follows them both, through one morning that cannot be taken back and the long years after it, from a roof in Afghanistan to a casino floor in Las Vegas, where the eye in the sky is a black glass dome.
It is a story about watching, and about what happens on the day the watched man finally looks back.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

This book began with one phrase. The military calls it pattern of life: watching a person long enough to learn what is normal for them, so that anything strange stands out. I wanted to know what that watching does to the one who watches, and what it looks like from the roof.
Nasim, Kayla and their families are invented, as are the strike in Maidan Shahr, the casino and the man in the gray jacket. Everything around them I tried to keep true.

The rules in Kayla’s chapters are the real ones. The 2013 standard of near certainty that no civilian would be hurt was real, and it did not apply in Afghanistan, which the United States counted as an area of active hostilities. In 2019, according to U.S. Air Forces Central Command, American aircraft released 7,423 weapons over Afghanistan, the most since its records began in 2006.

The strike in Kabul on 29 August 2021 is real. Ten people were killed, seven of them children. It was called a tragic mistake, and no one was punished. I took nothing from that family but the fact of it.

The question of guilt I tried not to answer. A survey of about a thousand Air Force drone operators, by psychologists at the Air Force School of Aerospace Medicine, found 4.3 percent with moderate to severe post-traumatic stress, and many proud of protecting the soldiers on the ground. The book has one of each. I do not know which is healthier.

The condolence payment is real in kind. The Pentagon reported that its payments in Afghanistan and Iraq in 2019 ranged from 169 dollars to 35,000, each one stated not to be an admission of responsibility.
The title is Nasim’s. A man waiting for his bird is the most innocent thing in this book, and it is also the habit that marked him. Seen from the sky, the two look exactly the same.
Chew Z
I. FORTY-ONE MORNINGS
ONE · Kayla
The war starts at six in the evening, forty-five minutes up Highway 95, and it has a parking lot.

That’s the first thing nobody tells you. You think of war, you think of sand and helicopters and some poor kid from Ohio with his legs gone. You don’t think of finding a space between a Silverado and a Kia Soul with a Baby On Board sticker, checking your lipstick in the mirror, and thinking, shit, I forgot to take the chicken out.

Creech Air Force Base sits in the desert outside a town called Indian Springs. It’s where the drones are flown from. Not where they fly. The aircraft is in Afghanistan, seven and a half thousand miles away, a gray plane with no window in its nose because nobody sits in it. We sit here, in Nevada, in a box.

The Air Force calls the box a Ground Control Station. Everybody else calls it the box. It’s a metal trailer with the air conditioning set to meat-locker, two chairs, a wall of screens, and a smell of burnt coffee and somebody’s body spray that has been in there since the Bush administration. The pilot sits in the left chair and flies the plane. I sit in the right chair. I’m the sensor operator, which means I fly the camera. I decide what we look at. And when it’s time, I hold the laser on the target, a little invisible finger of light that tells the missile where to go.
He drives. I point.

The plane is an MQ-9 Reaper, like the guy with the hood and the scythe, because somebody in the office that buys the weapons thought that was cute. It can stay up for more than a day, and it carries four Hellfire missiles under its wings like a woman carrying grocery bags. From where it circles, three miles up, it can read the shape of a man’s sandal. I know this because I have read a lot of sandals.

My name is Kayla Rourke. I’m thirty-one. I have a seven-year-old son named Wyatt who believes I fly airplanes, which is true in the way most things you tell a seven-year-old are true. I have a mother in Henderson who believes I’m going to Hell, which is also probably true. I have a mouth on me. My first sergeant once told me I curse like a Navy cook with a toothache, and I told him to go fuck himself, and he laughed, and that was the last nice thing that happened in that building.

You show your ID to a nineteen-year-old with a rifle, you put your phone in a little locker because phones aren’t allowed near the war, you walk down a hallway with carpet the color of old gum, and you sit in your chair.
And then it’s morning.

That’s the second thing nobody tells you. Afghanistan is eleven and a half hours ahead of Las Vegas, so I leave the house in the late afternoon and walk into dawn. I have watched more sunrises over Afghanistan than over Nevada.

I’ve watched them in two colors. The daylight camera is just like your phone, only it’s three miles up and it can count the buttons on a shirt. The other one is the infrared, the heat camera. It doesn’t see light. It sees warmth. Everything warmer than the world around it glows.
You can set it two ways. Black hot, where the warm things are dark. Or white hot, where the warm things shine.

I like white hot. Most of us do. In white hot, a man is a candle walking. A cow is a lamp. An engine that ran an hour ago is a smear of milk on the road. A cup of tea held in two hands makes a little bright coin against a chest. The world is gray and cold and the living are made of light.
White means warm. Warm means alive.

They teach you that on day one, in the schoolhouse, before they teach you anything else. They teach it like a joke. It isn’t a joke. It’s the whole job. Everything else is just deciding which of the lights to put out.

The pilot was a man I’ll call the pilot, because that’s what he was. A captain, with a wife and three girls and a boat at Lake Mead named after his wife, which tells you most of what you need to know. He coached Little League on Saturdays. He ate the same turkey sandwich every shift with the crusts cut off, and he slept, as far as I could ever tell, like a baby in a car seat.
“Morning, sunshine,” he said, which is what he said every night.
“Fuck off,” I said, which is what I said every night.

There’s a lag, and you should know about it now, because it matters later. The signal goes from the box to a satellite, to Europe, to another satellite, to the plane. It takes about a second and a half. You move the stick, and a second and a half later, over Afghanistan, the camera moves. You learn to live a second and a half in the future. You learn to lead everything. People say drone crews play God. We don’t. God doesn’t lag.
That night, the outgoing operator, a kid named Torres, handed me a house.
“New package,” he said. “Wardak province. Town called Maidan Shahr.”

He said it MAY-den SHAR. The real way is more like [mai-DAAN SHAHR], and it means the City of the Square. Wardak is [war-DAK]. I looked it all up, later. It’s a provincial capital west of Kabul [KAA-bul], in a valley with mountains on both sides like a pair of hands about to clap.
“Selector’s living there,” Torres said.

A selector is a phone number. That’s all. A string of digits that belongs to somebody somebody else wants dead. Intelligence people, a long way up from us, decide a phone belongs to a bad guy. Then they track it. Wherever the phone sleeps, we watch. People think we hunt men. Mostly we hunt phones. The men are attached.
“Facilitator,” Torres said. “Moves money, moves guys. Medium fish. Phone’s been sleeping in this house four nights out of the last six.”

It was a house like ten thousand other houses down there. A square of mud-brick wall around a little courtyard. A tree in the courtyard. A flat roof, with stairs running up the outside. A blue metal door to the street. And on the roof, a sort of cabinet made of wire and wood.
“What’s the cage,” I said.
“Chickens, probably,” Torres said. “They all got chickens.”
That was the first day.
Here’s what I want you to understand, before you hate me, which you will, and before you forgive me, which you shouldn’t.
I liked the house.

I liked it the way you like a show you watch while folding laundry. I watched it twelve hours a night, which was twelve hours of their day, and I got to know it the way you know your own kitchen. I knew which corner of the courtyard got the sun first. I knew the tree was a mulberry, because in the second week the ground under it went dark and sticky with fallen fruit, and the kids from next door came and ate it off the dirt. I knew the blue door stuck, because everybody who opened it put their shoulder into it.
I knew there was a man, and a woman, and a little girl.
The man was on the roof every morning at first light. Every single morning. He opened the cage. And then he stood there on the roof, in the cold blue start of the day, with his face turned up.
Up. At the sky.
At me.
That’s what I thought. God help me. That’s what I wrote down.

But that comes later. The first day, all I did was what they trained me to do. I set the camera to white hot. I zoomed in until the house filled the screen. I watched three small fires moving behind its walls, a big one and a medium one and a little one, and I thought, like a prayer or a curse:
White means warm. Warm means alive.
And I started counting.
TWO · Nasim
Before the town wakes, there is a sound that comes before all other sounds, and that is the sound of the birds asking to be let out.

It is not a song. Pigeons do not sing. It is a kind of talking, low and round, made in the chest, hoo-oo, hoo-oo, as if the bird were a little drum struck by someone very patient. My father used to say the pigeons talk to God before anyone else is awake, and that they only ever ask Him one question: Is it time?

My name is Nasim Nazari [na-SEEM na-zaa-REE]. Nasim means a breeze, the small cool wind that comes just before morning. My mother chose it because I was born at dawn, and she said I came into the world the way that wind comes, quietly, and wanting to be outside.

I have kept pigeons for thirty-one years. I am a kaftar-baz [kaf-TAR BAAZ]. The word means a pigeon player, and it is not quite a compliment. In our country, a kaftar-baz is a man who is up on his roof when he should be at his work, and who looks at the sky when he should be looking at his family. My wife, Laila [lay-LAA], says this about me often, and she is not wrong, and she says it smiling, and so I have never stopped.

Our house is in Maidan Shahr, in the province of Wardak, an hour’s drive west of Kabul if the road is good, and three hours if the road is the road. My father built it of mud brick and timber, and I helped him by carrying water in a tin cup when I was too small to carry anything else. There is a mulberry tree in the courtyard that my mother planted the year I was born. There is a blue door to the street that has stuck since before my daughter was born, which I promise every spring to fix, and have not fixed, because a door that sticks is a door that tells you when someone is coming.
On the roof is the loft, the house of the birds. I built it with my own hands from wire and the wood of old fruit crates. It has twenty-two small rooms.
Let me tell you how it is done, the flying of the birds. It is the most beautiful thing I know, and I am the only one left who can tell you.

At first light I climb the outside stairs, which are cold under my feet even in summer. Below me the town is still blue, the color of milk in a dark kitchen. The mountains on either side of the valley are black, and above them the sky is the color that has no name, not yet white and no longer night. Somewhere a rooster complains. Somewhere a pot is set down on a stone.

I open the loft. First come the old ones, the ones who know the way, because they will teach the young. They sit at the edge a moment, blinking, settling their feathers, looking at the sky the way an old man looks at the sea. Then one of them, always the same one, an old gray male with a white collar whom my daughter named Uncle, steps off the edge and drops.
He drops like a stone for the length of my arm. And then the wings open.

The sound of a pigeon’s wings opening is like a book slammed shut by a child. Clap. And then the others follow, clap clap clap clap, out over the courtyard and over the wall, and they turn, all together, as if they were one bird with twenty-two hearts. No one leads. No one gives an order. They simply turn. And in the turning the light catches all their undersides at once, and the whole flock flashes white, like a hand opening.

Then they go up, in circles, wider and higher, until they are no longer birds, only a kind of glitter, a handful of salt thrown at the sky. And you keep watching, because the whole art of it is in the coming down. A good flock comes home. A bad flock goes to another man’s roof.
So you stand. And you look up. And you wait for them to come back to you.
This is what I do every morning of my life.

My daughter is called Parisa [pa-ree-SAA]. It means like a fairy, which she is not. She is like a goat. She is eight years old and climbs everything that can be climbed and some things that cannot. She has a gap in her front teeth where a new one is coming, and she whistles through it, badly, all day, until her mother sends her outside.

She has a pair of sandals I bought her in the bazaar in Kabul, pink plastic with a yellow plastic flower on each toe, and she loves them more than she loves either of her parents. She will not let them be taken off her feet even when she sleeps. She will be buried in her sandals, Laila said to me once, laughing, and I laughed too, and God forgive us both.

Most mornings she comes up the outside stairs in those sandals, slap, slap, slap, and stands next to me with her head back, though she does not know what she is looking for, and says, “Where are they, Baba?” Baba [BAA-baa] is what our children call their fathers.
“Up,” I say.
“I can’t see them.”
“That is because they are very good. The good ones go so high that only God and I can see them.”
“You can’t see them either.”
“No,” I say. “But I know where they are.”
And she puts her small hand in mine, which is cold from the stairs, and we stand on the roof together and look up at the sky.
That is how He saw us, I suppose, if He was looking. A man and a girl on a roof at dawn with their faces turned up, as if they were waiting for something to come down.

I fix things. Radios, televisions, and now telephones, because there is not a family in Maidan Shahr without a telephone, and not a telephone in Maidan Shahr that does not break. I have a shop in the bazaar the size of a horse stall, with a table and a lamp and a soldering iron my father bought from a Russian soldier for a sack of rice, in a year I do not want to remember.
The shop opens when the birds come down. That is my rule.
That summer, the summer I am telling you about, we were happy.

I want to say this clearly. Afterwards, people tell the story of a family like mine as if it were always going to end the way it ended. As if we were walking toward it the whole time with our heads down. We were not. We were three people in a house with a sticking door and a mulberry tree. Laila sewed dresses for the women of the street on a black Chinese sewing machine with a gold dragon painted on its side. Parisa went to the girls’ school by the river and climbed the mulberry tree in the afternoons. In the evenings we drank green tea in the courtyard, and when the heat came we carried our mattresses up to the roof and slept under the stars, as everyone does in summer, because the house holds the heat of the day like a hand holds a stone.
We were happy. We did not know it. That is the only way to be happy. If you know it, you are already afraid.
And that summer, there was the sound.

I do not know when it began. It came the way the summer heat comes, a little at a time, until one day you notice you have been sweating for a week. A high, thin, faraway buzzing, like a mosquito trapped in another room. You heard it most at night, and at dawn, when the town was quiet. It came from nowhere, and from up.

Everyone knew what it was. No one said it. By that summer, the children in our part of the country could tell you the sounds of the sky the way children elsewhere can tell you the names of footballers. This is a helicopter. This is a jet, too high to matter. This is the other thing, the one you cannot see, that goes around and around and never lands.
Parisa called it the mosquito.
“Baba, the mosquito’s back,” she would say on the roof at night, lying between Laila and me with her sandals on.
“It’s not for us.”
“How do you know?”
“Because we are nobody,” I said. “It is looking for somebody.”

That was what everybody believed. That it was looking for the bad men in the mountains, the ones with guns, the ones in the trucks. That it had no interest in a man with a soldering iron and twenty-two birds. That if you were nobody, you were safe, because nobody was invisible.

So in the mornings, when I stood on the roof and waited for my birds and the sound was there, I did what you do when a stranger stands across the street watching your house. I did not hide. Hiding is what guilty men do.
I looked up at it.
I nodded to it, the way you nod to a neighbor.
Good morning, I said in my heart. I am only a kaftar-baz. I am only waiting for my birds.
THREE · Kayla
People think you just push a button.

You don’t. I want that on the record before anything else is. There are rules. There are so many rules they come in binders, and there’s a guy at the schoolhouse whose whole job is to make you say them back to him like the Pledge of Allegiance. Let me tell you the rules. Not because they’ll make you feel better. Because they made me feel better, for a while, and I want you to see how.

Rule one is positive identification. They call it PID. It means you have to know who you’re looking at. Not think. Know. Before anybody fires anything, somebody has to be able to say: that man is the person on the list. And if there’s any doubt about whether somebody is a civilian, the rule says you treat them as one. That’s the law. When in doubt, he’s a farmer. No PID, no strike. The instructor said it so many times it turned into one word, like a spell.

Rule two is the collateral damage estimate. Collateral damage is the military way of saying everybody else. The wife. The kid. The guy selling cigarettes on the wrong corner. Before a strike, somebody sits down with a map and a set of tables and works out who else gets hurt if this missile hits that spot. How big the blast is. Whether the wall is mud or concrete. Whether the room next door has people in it, and how many, and when they go to sleep. You don’t do the math. But you feed it. You’re the one who says, two adults and a child sleep in the back room, east side, lights out around ten. You’re the eyes the math is built on. They told us the chance of hurting anybody who isn’t the target has to come out under ten percent.

Rule three is the rules of engagement: who is allowed to say yes. In Afghanistan, that year, the yes didn’t come from me or the pilot. It came from a commander somewhere else. A lawyer read the package. The commander signed it. We were the hands at the end of a long arm.
Rule four doesn’t have a name. Rule four is: You are not a killer. You are a link.

Nobody said that one out loud. They didn’t need to. It was in the way the whole thing was built. Intelligence finds the phone. Analysts in another state, called screeners, watch the same video I watch and say what they see. The mission intelligence coordinator, the MIC, who sits behind us with a headset and a laptop and a permanent cold, puts it together. The lawyer checks it. The commander signs. The pilot flies. I point.
Nobody kills anybody. Everybody does a little piece.
It’s a good feeling. That’s what I want you to understand. It’s like carrying a coffin with six other people, where nobody’s arm does all the work, and nobody’s arm is to blame for how heavy it is.
The other thing they teach you is pattern of life. It’s what I did to that house for forty-one days.

It means you watch somebody until you know their life better than they do. When they wake. When they eat. Who comes to the door, what they carry, where they go and whether they come back the same way. You learn what normal is for that house, and then you look for the thing that isn’t.
You’d be amazed what you know after a month.

I knew the woman. I never saw her face, because she covered it when she went out, and in the courtyard the tree was in the way. But she worked at something in a ground-floor room that made her bend over a table for hours, and in the late afternoon she’d come out and stand with both hands on the small of her back and stretch, and I’d stretch too, in my chair, without thinking, like a yawn going around a room.

I knew the girl. From three miles up I could see her shoes. Pink sandals, with a dot of yellow on the toe. She wore them up the tree. She wore them on the roof at night, when they all slept up there in the heat, three white shapes in a row, a big one and a medium one and a little one, like a goddamn bedtime story.

And I knew the man. He walked with his right shoulder a little lower than his left, like he’d spent his life carrying something on that side. He had a shop in the bazaar, a little hole in a long row of little holes. In the evenings men came to his courtyard, one or two at a time, and drank tea, and left. And the phone was still there.
The phone. The selector. It slept at his house most nights. And here’s what made the MIC stop sniffing for once: in the mornings, the phone went up to the roof. The man goes up, the phone goes up.
“What’s he doing up there,” the MIC said.
“Chickens,” I said, because that’s what Torres had said.
The MIC zoomed his own screen. They weren’t chickens. They were too small, and they were up on little shelves in the wire.
“Pigeons,” the pilot said, with his mouth full of turkey sandwich. “My granddad kept pigeons. For racing. People used to send messages with them.”

And there it was. Nobody said it. It came into the room the way the cold came in, through the vents, and settled on us. Messages. A man who sleeps with a bad guy’s phone, takes it to the roof every morning, and keeps the birds people used to send messages with.

Not one of us thought he was sending messages by pigeon. It was 2019. But it went into the picture anyway. A little gray smudge in the corner of a painting that you’d swear wasn’t there, and that changes the whole thing.
I’d get home around seven in the morning. Wyatt would be eating cereal at the counter in his dinosaur pajamas, and I’d stand in the kitchen with my keys still in my hand and do the stupidest thing.
I’d count him.
One. Big as a lamp. Warm.
“Mom, you smell like the airplane,” he’d say.
“Airplanes don’t smell, dummy.”
“Yours does.”
He was right. The box got into your hair.

Then I’d lie down in the dark with the blackout curtains closed and a fan going for the noise, and behind my eyelids the house would be there. The blue door. The tree. The man on the roof with his face turned up. Like a song stuck in your head. Like when you’ve driven all day and lie down and still feel the road moving under you.
That’s all it was. I didn’t feel bad. Not then. I want to be clear, so you know I’m not lying to make myself look better. I was doing my job, and I was good at it, and I liked being good at it.
I liked the house. I’ll say it again, because it’s the worst thing in this whole story, and nobody ever believes it.
I liked them.
FOUR · Nasim
A telephone is a little box full of other people.

My father taught me this, though he never saw a mobile telephone in his life. He said it of radios. Be gentle when you open a radio, Nasim, because inside it are a thousand people who have not finished talking.
I do not believe this. But I open them gently. You never know.

That summer I had more telephones than I had ever had. They came to me in plastic bags and handkerchiefs and the pockets of men who had walked two days from the villages to the south. Cracked faces. Dead batteries. Charging holes full of sand.

The ones I could not finish in the shop, I took home. Laila did not like it. She said I brought the bazaar into the house. But the shop had one lamp and a generator that coughed like an old man, and the house had better light, and green tea. So in the evenings I sat under the mulberry tree with a tray of broken telephones on my knees, and Parisa sat beside me and handed me the tiny screws, which she kept in the lid of a jam jar and counted out loud.
“Twelve,” she said. “Baba, why does it need twelve screws?”
“So that it does not fall apart.”
“I don’t have twelve screws.”
“You have more,” I said. “You have a hundred. They are inside, where no one can see them.”
She looked at her arm very hard, as if she might see them.

After I fixed a telephone, I had to test it. In Maidan Shahr the signal comes and goes like a cat. In the courtyard it would not come at all. The only place it was always strong was the roof. So every night, and every morning when I went up to the birds, I carried the telephones up in a cloth bag and set them in a row on the low wall at the edge of the roof, like children waiting for the school bus, and watched their little screens light up as they found the tower on the hill.
This is how a telephone tells you it is alive. A small light. A bar, two bars, three.
I did not know that someone was counting the same bars.
That summer, a young man came to the shop. I have thought about him every day since, and I still do not know what to think.

He was perhaps twenty-five, with a short beard and very clean hands. He did not give me his name, and I did not ask. In our country, in those years, you did not ask a man’s name if he did not offer it. It was a way of keeping each other alive.

His telephone was a cheap black Samsung with a cracked back held together with tape. The charging hole was broken. I fixed it, and he paid me more than I asked. A week later he came back, and the hole was broken again, and he left it with me again. That happened three times, four times, that summer. Each time I took it home. Each time it slept on my wall, in the row, with the others.
I never looked at what was inside it. The names. The calls. That is the first rule of a man who fixes telephones, the same as a doctor’s or a priest’s. You do not read the letters in the box.

Once he brought Parisa a sweet wrapped in green paper. She ate it in one bite and asked for another, and Laila scolded her for asking, and the young man laughed. He laughed with his whole face, the way young men do before they learn not to.

I know now what they thought he was. I have read it in English, on paper, with a seal on top. But I do not know who he was. A man who laughs with his whole face at a little girl asking for a second sweet. A man whose telephone, they say, belonged to men who sent other men to die. Maybe he was both. Maybe most men are.
“The birds are enough,” Laila said. “Now you have telephones sleeping with the birds.”
“Laila,” I said. “Qatra qatra darya mesha [KAT-ra KAT-ra DAR-ya mee-SHA].”

It is an old saying of ours: drop by drop, a river is made. Every telephone I fixed at home was a little more money, and every little more was for Parisa, for a real school in Kabul one day, with a library, for a girl who counted screws and asked why.
Laila looked at me the way she did when I was being clever.
“Drop by drop,” she said, “a river is made. And drop by drop, a roof falls in.”

That is not a saying. She made it up. She was always making up sayings and pretending they were old, and fooling the women of the street with them. She meant only that the roof was old and I was putting too much on it: birds, telephones, a grown man, a growing girl.
I laughed.

I have thought about that sentence more than any sentence in my life, including the ones in the Holy Book. I know it was a joke about a roof. I know that God does not speak through the jokes of seamstresses.
I know it.
FIVE · Kayla
Day thirty-three.

I remember because I wrote it at the top of the page. I wrote everything down. That was the job. You watch, you write. Time, what you saw, what it might mean. It was called the log, and it went up the chain: the MIC, the screeners, the intel people, the lawyer, the commander. Everybody read my log. My log was the house. Nobody up the chain had been there.
That’s a hell of a thing to be. The only one who knows somebody.

By day thirty-three the picture had a shape. That’s how the intelligence people talk about it. Building a picture, like a puzzle on a card table at your grandma’s house. Here are the pieces, the way they went up the chain:
The selector sleeps at the house, most nights.
The selector goes to the roof every morning at first light, with the man.
Military-age males visit in the evenings, alone or in pairs, for under an hour.
The man carries sacks up to the roof two or three times a week. Contents unknown.
The man stands on the roof every morning and looks at the sky.
Now the other way. The way I’d tell it to you on my couch with a beer.

He fixes phones, you idiot. He tests them on the roof because that’s where the signal is. The men in the evenings are customers, or neighbors, drinking tea, because in that part of the world they drink tea at you until you die. The sacks are bird feed. The looking up is him watching his birds.
I know that now. But here’s what I need you to understand, or nothing else in this book will make sense.
I could have seen it then.

Every piece had a second face, a harmless one, and any of us could have turned it over. Nobody did. Not because we were evil, or stupid. Because of the way a picture builds. Once the first piece goes down, the next one fits beside it. You stop asking what each piece is. You start asking where it goes. There’s a name for it, I found out later, in a book a shrink gave me: confirmation bias. Once you believe a thing, your brain goes looking for proof and walks right past everything that says you’re wrong. Everybody does it. You did it at breakfast.
We just did it with a Hellfire.
And the birds.
This is the part I’ve never told anyone. Not the investigators. Not the shrink. Not my mother.

Some mornings, in the daylight camera, I saw something over the house. A gray flicker, a little cloud of grain that rose and spun and caught the light and went white and then gray and then white again, all at once, like somebody shaking out a sheet. It went up in circles until it was gone.
I saw it more than once. I thought: dust. I thought: a glitch, the satellite hiccuping. I thought: birds, maybe.
I didn’t zoom out.

The camera was on the man. That’s where you keep it. They teach you the camera is a straw, not a window. You only see what you point it at. I had it pointed at a man on a roof, so what I saw was a man on a roof with his face turned up.
And I wrote, in the log, on day thirty-three, at 0544 local time, in the small block capitals they taught us so nobody could misread anything:
SUBJECT ON ROOF. LOOKS UP AT AIRCRAFT AT DAWN, DAILY. POSSIBLE AWARENESS OF SURVEILLANCE.

You have to understand what that means, up the chain. Nobody innocent looks up. That’s the thinking. Farmers look at the ground. Shopkeepers look at the street. A man who goes up on his roof every morning and looks right at you is a man who knows what’s up there and is checking it’s still there.
That’s what I meant. God help me. That’s exactly what I meant.
The MIC read it and said, “Huh,” and typed something into his laptop.
The pilot said, “Creepy,” and went back to his sandwich.

I sat there with the camera on the man, and the man stood with his face turned up at me, and for one second, with the lag, it felt like he was a second and a half ahead of me. Like he’d already seen me, and I was only now seeing him seeing me.
I waved. I don’t know why. A little wave with two fingers, below the desk where nobody could see, like you’d wave at a baby through a car window.
He didn’t wave back. He couldn’t see me. He was looking at his birds.
Things moved after that, slowly and then fast. The package went up. Nominated was the word, like an Oscar. The lawyer read it. The commander, whoever he was, read my log.
And the math came back with a plan, and here’s the part that will make you sick.
The plan was the dawn.

The best time to strike, the math said, is when the man is alone on the roof. Most nights that summer the three of them slept up there together, so the plan carried a condition: the first dawn the wife and the girl were below, in the back room on the east side, where the log said they went when they came down. A small missile, the kind made for exactly this, aimed at the man on the roof at first light. The blast stays on the roof. The people under it are outside the circle. The chance of hurting them comes out under the line.

It was the most careful plan I ever saw. It was built out of my log. It knew the man was on that roof every morning at first light, because I’d told it. It knew where the woman and the child slept, because I’d told it. It was designed, every inch of it, to kill him and nobody else.
To protect them. That’s what it was for.
You understand? The thing that marked him was his habit of standing on that roof, and the thing that was supposed to save his family was his habit of standing on that roof.
Every morning. Without fail.
Never once, in thirty-three days, had he missed.
SIX · Nasim
On the fortieth night we slept on the roof that summer, the wind came.

We had been sleeping on the roof for weeks. You carry up the thin cotton mattresses in the evening and lay them in a row, and lie with your face to the sky, and the stars are so many and so close you feel you could put one in your pocket. You hear the whole town settling. A donkey. A radio. A mother calling a child in for the last time. Then only the dogs, and the crickets, and that summer, the sound.
Parisa lay between us. She always did. She said it was the safest place in Afghanistan, and I told her she was right.
“Baba,” she said. “The mosquito.”
“I hear it.”
“Is it looking at us?”
“It is like the moon,” I said. “It looks at everyone, and so it looks at no one.”
She was quiet a while. You could always hear her thinking. Her breath changed.
“Tell me the bird story.”

There is a story in our old book, the Shahnameh [SHAAH-naa-meh], the Book of Kings, a thousand years old, which every child in our part of the world knows in pieces. In it there is a bird called the Simorgh [see-MORGH].

She is as big as a cloud, and very old, and very wise, and she lives at the top of a mountain so high no man has ever climbed it. From there she sees everything. Every valley. Every house. Every child.

Once, a king had a baby son born with white hair, white as an old man’s, and the king was ashamed, and left the baby at the foot of the mountain to die. And the Simorgh saw. She came down and lifted the baby gently in her claws and raised him in her nest with her own children. His name was Zal [ZAAL]. When he was grown and wanted to go down the mountain and live among men, she gave him three of her feathers. If ever you are in danger, she said, burn one, and wherever I am, I will see the smoke, and I will come.
I told it to her every night that summer, and every night she asked the same questions, and I gave the same answers.
“Did he burn the feathers?”
“He did, when his wife was dying. And the Simorgh came, and saved them both.”
“So the Simorgh watches us?”
“The Simorgh watches everyone. That is her job.”
That night, the fortieth night, she asked a new question.
“Baba. Is the mosquito a Simorgh?”
I lay there with the sound going around and around above us, high and thin and patient, and I thought about it.
“No,” I said.
“How do you know?”
“Because the Simorgh comes down. That is the whole point of her. She watches, and when you need her, she comes down. The mosquito only watches.”
“Maybe it will come down.”
“Maybe,” I said. “Go to sleep, jan [JAAN].”
Jan means life. It is what we call the ones we love. Parisa-jan. My life.
After midnight the wind came over the mountains from the west, bringing the dust, the way it does at the end of summer. Not a storm. Only a gritty wind that gets into your teeth and your eyes.
Laila sat up and coughed. “I’m taking her down.”
“Leave her. It will pass.”
“It’s in her mouth, Nasim. I’m taking her down.”

So she lifted Parisa, who did not wake, who was too heavy now to be lifted and was lifted anyway, the way mothers do, with a small grunt. Parisa’s sandals dangled from her feet, pink, with the yellow flowers. Laila carried her down the outside stairs, slowly, in the dark, and I heard the door of the house stick and then give, and then I heard nothing.
They slept in the back room, on the east side, where it is coolest. They always did, when they came down.
I stayed on the roof.
I could have gone down. I think of that. I could have rolled up my mattress and slept on the floor of the back room with my wife and daughter, and been there, under the roof, with them.

But the birds were restless in the wind, hoo-oo, hoo-oo, worried, and I did not want to leave them. So I lay down again, alone, with my scarf over my face against the grit, and I listened to the wind and the birds and the sound, and I slept.
I woke at first light. My body knows the hour better than any clock.

The wind had gone. The air was washed and cold and very clear, as if someone had wiped the whole sky with a wet cloth. The mountains were black. The town was blue. The sky over the eastern ridge was the color that has no name.
I folded my mattress and set it by the stairs. I opened the loft.
Uncle came to the edge and looked at me with one orange eye, as he did every morning, as if to ask, Is it time?
“It’s time,” I said.

He stepped off and dropped, and the wings opened. Clap. And the others went after him, out over the mulberry tree, and they turned, and in the first light from the east the flock flashed white all at once, like a hand opening.
I stood with my head back and watched them rise, wider and higher, until they were a handful of salt.
The sound was there. High and thin and patient.
I looked up at it. I nodded.
Good morning, I said in my heart. I am only a kaftar-baz.
I am only waiting for my birds.
INTERLUDE ONE · 1861–1863
A Short History of Watching from Above
The Man in the Basket

This is a true story, from the first American war in which an army watched its enemy from the sky. It is about the oldest part of a drone strike, the part that comes before everything else: the looking.
In the summer of 1861, the United States was at war with itself, and Washington was a nervous city, close enough to the enemy that on a clear day you could almost feel them across the river.

A balloonist named Thaddeus Lowe had an idea. What if a man went up in a balloon, tied to the ground by a rope, and simply looked? Generals had always had to guess what was on the other side of the hill. From high enough, a man could see over every hill at once, and count the enemy’s tents and cannons, and watch which way they marched.

In June 1861, Lowe rose over Washington with a telegraph wire running down the rope, and from the sky he sent a message to President Lincoln. It said, more or less: I can see for fifty miles in every direction. It was the first time anyone had sent words straight down from the sky. Soon Lowe’s balloons were following the Union Army from battle to battle, with men hanging in wicker baskets in the cold, watching, and sending down what they saw.
Here is the part that matters to this book.
The men in the baskets could be seen.

A balloon is a very large thing. The soldiers below could see it hanging over their camp like a second moon. On a clear day they could see the man in the basket. And they did what soldiers do: they fired at him. The watcher and the watched could see each other, and each could kill the other.
That was the bargain, in the beginning. If you want to watch a man from above, you have to let him look back at you.
Two years later, in the same war, under the same president, something else happened that almost nobody connects to the balloons.

In April 1863, Lincoln signed a set of written rules for how his soldiers must behave. It was called the Lieber Code [LEE-ber], after the professor who wrote it, and it was one of the first times any army wrote its rules down. Among many things, it said that unarmed citizens should be spared, as much as the needs of war allowed.
As much as the needs of war allowed. Somebody always has to decide what the needs of war allow, and who is unarmed.
Who decides? And how would a man in a basket, a mile up, tell a farmer from a soldier who had put down his rifle to eat?

In the same war, signed by the same hand, came the first eye in the sky and the first written promise to protect people who are not fighting. One was a way of seeing everything. The other was a promise about what you would do with what you saw. It would take them a hundred and fifty years to meet.
The Balloon Corps did not last. By the summer of 1863, the balloons were packed away.

But before they were, a Southern boy in a gray coat looked up from his campfire in a field in Virginia and saw one hanging above the trees. He could see the basket, and the small dark shape of the man in it, leaning over the edge with a spyglass, or a pencil, or only his own two hands holding on. For a moment the two of them looked at each other across the empty air. A man looking down. A man looking up. Each could see the other. Each could, if he wanted, try to kill the other.
They were equals, for that one moment.
The boy raised his hand to shade his eyes. Maybe he meant it as a salute. Maybe he meant nothing at all.
It was the last time the watched would see the watcher’s face.
II. BUGSPLAT
SEVEN · Kayla
The chicken.
I want to start with the chicken, because that’s where the day started, and because for a long time afterwards it was the only part of the day I could stand to think about.

I woke at ten past one in the afternoon with the blackout curtains closed and the fan going and my mouth tasting like a penny. The light around the edges of the curtains was that hard white Las Vegas light that looks less like daylight than a fluorescent tube somebody left on in God’s garage.
And I thought: the chicken.

I’d bought a pack of thighs on Sunday, family size, on sale, and every day that week I’d meant to take them out of the freezer in the morning, and every day I’d come home from killing nobody and gone straight to bed and forgotten. So that was the first thing I did on the day. I went into the kitchen in a T-shirt and underwear and put the frozen thighs in the sink in a bowl of cold water, the way my mother taught me, because she said only white trash thawed meat in the microwave.
I stood there and watched the water go cloudy around the plastic.
That’s the last clean memory. The chicken in the bowl in the sink. The water turning white.

Wyatt was at school until three. I did the laundry. A seven-year-old boy makes laundry like he’s training for something. Grass stains, ketchup, a sock that had been in a puddle and then in the hamper for a week and had become something new, with its own opinions. His dino-jammies, though he’d started telling me he was too old for that word. The socks that didn’t match went into the Basket of Lonely Socks, which is a real basket in my house, and which Wyatt named, and which he checks every week like a lost and found.
I folded his clothes and I didn’t think about Afghanistan.

That’s not a brag. People think you carry it around all day. You can’t. Your hands do small things and your mind does small things, and the war sits in a box in the desert forty-five minutes away, waiting for you, the way the office waits for anybody.

On the counter was a permission slip. Second grade was going to the Hoover Dam. I signed it, checked no for allergies, put a ten and a one in the envelope for the bus, and licked it, and it tasted like glue and summer. I’d lived in Vegas six years and never been to the Hoover Dam. I thought: I should go with them. I should ask for a day.
I put the envelope in the front pocket of his backpack, where he’d find it.

My mother called at two-fifteen. She calls every Wednesday. She lives in Henderson with a man named Gary who sells pool chemicals, and she believes, with her whole heart, that I am in the business of murder and that Jesus will forgive me if I ask Him nicely.
“Are you eating,” she said.
“I’m thawing chicken.”
“In the sink?”
“In the sink, Mom.”
“Good girl.” And then, the way you’d say drive safe: “Are you going to kill anybody today?”
“I don’t kill anybody, Mom. I point a camera.”
“Well,” she said, “point it nice.”
She laughed. I laughed. It had been our joke for two years. It was the worst joke in the world and we both knew it, and that was why it worked. You can say anything if you say it like it’s funny.

I didn’t know. I want to tell you I felt something, a shadow, a chill. I didn’t. The package had gone up the chain two days before and was sitting on some desk, waiting for some signature, and nobody tells the sensor operator when the signature comes. They tell you when you sit down.

I picked Wyatt up at three. He got in the back with his face red from the playground and told me without stopping for breath that a kid named Jaden had eaten a whole blue crayon and his poop was going to be blue.
“Gross,” I said.
“I know,” he said, delighted.

I made him a grilled cheese, cut in triangles. I put the chicken in a dish with lemon and garlic and salt and left a note for the sitter: 350 for 40 min. Make him eat a vegetable. A pickle counts. We did his spelling words. That week they all ended in -ight. Light. Night. Bright. Right. Fight. Sight. He spelled sight like site. I told him that was a different word, a place where something happens, like a building site. He said two words that sound the same and mean different things was stupid. I said that was English.
The sitter came at four-thirty. I kissed Wyatt on the top of the head, which smelled like crayons and grilled cheese and boy.
“Bye, Mom. Fly the airplane.”
“I’ll fly it.”
“Fly it high.”
“Always,” I said.

On the drive up, the sun was behind me and the desert was the color of a lion. Highway 95 runs northwest out of Las Vegas straight as a ruler, mountains on the left getting closer and redder, dry lake beds on the right as flat and white as spilled flour. There are things I remember about that drive that I have no business remembering. A hawk on a telephone pole. A white Corolla on a donut spare. Ninety-four degrees on the dashboard. The steering wheel too hot to hold at the top, so I drove with my hands at the bottom, like a teenager.
The pilot was already in his chair with his turkey sandwich unwrapped on his knee.
“Morning, sunshine,” he said.
And then, before I could tell him to fuck off: “It came through.”
That’s all. It came through. The way you’d say a check had cleared.

Torres gave me his chair and the brief. Fuel, weapons, weather. Clear sky, light wind from the west, dropping. The dust that had come through in the night had blown out. It was going to be a beautiful morning in Maidan Shahr.
“Package approved,” he said. “Execute at first light. Target on the roof, alone, PID holds.” He clapped me on the shoulder. “Your boy, Rourke. You found him.”
Your boy.
I sat down.

On the screen it was a quarter past five in the morning. The house was where it always was, the courtyard dark, the tree a black puff. In white hot, the roof glowed faintly, the bricks still holding a little of yesterday’s heat. And on the roof, near the cage, one white shape. Lying down. Alone.
“Where are the other two,” the MIC said, behind me.
I rolled back through the night crew’s notes and read it out. 0047L. Adult female and child move from roof to ground floor, east room. Wind.
“East room,” the MIC said. “Good. That’s outside the circle.”
“That’s outside the circle,” the pilot said, and took a bite of his sandwich.

And I sat with my hands on the controls and looked at the one white shape curled on its side, and I thought about the chicken in the oven forty-five minutes south, and the spelling words, and the eleven dollars in the front pocket of a backpack.
Light. Night. Bright. Right. Fight. Sight.
I thought: it’s just a morning.
I thought: he’s going to get up and go to the cage, the way he always does.
He always did.
EIGHT · Nasim
When the birds are up, there is a time that belongs to no one.

They are too high to watch and too soon to come down, a glitter somewhere over the eastern ridge, and you know they will not come home for half an hour. You cannot leave the roof, because you must be there when they return. My father called it the empty cup: the time after you have poured the tea and before it is cool enough to drink.
Most men fill the empty cup with nothing. I do the work of the loft. I will tell you what that work is, because it was the last work I did with that life, and I want somebody besides me to know it.
First, the water.

There is a shallow clay dish in the loft that collects dust and feathers in the night. I tipped it over the edge of the roof, the way I always did, and the water fell in one long rope and made a dark star in the dust of the street. Then I carried the dish down the outside stairs to the tap in the courtyard. The mulberry tree was full of sparrows, waking up and arguing. The tap coughed twice before it gave water, as if it had to remember, every morning, what water is. I filled the dish and carried it back up step by step, in both hands, like a man carrying a lamp.
Behind the door below me I could hear Laila. The scrape of the iron plate on the gas ring, the soft whump of the flame, the clink of the teapot lid. She coughed once, from the dust of the night.
“Up,” she said to Parisa. “Up, up. The school will not come to you.”
And Parisa, from under the blanket, in a voice like a cat being sat on: “Five minutes.”
Every child in the world says five minutes, in every language. I believe it is the first sentence God gave to children, before mother or father or bread.
Second, the floor.

I scraped the boards of the loft with a flat tin blade. It is a good sound, the scraper on the wood, a long dry sound like a man clearing his throat before he says something important. The loft smelled of birds, warm and dusty and a little sweet, like the inside of an old coat.

The town was waking. The baker on the corner had lit his tandoor [tan-DOOR], the round clay oven sunk into the ground, and the smell of the bread came over the wall, hot stone and flour, the smell of every morning of my life. A radio was playing the news from Kabul in a voice trying very hard to sound calm. A boy drove goats down the street, tapping their bony backs with a stick and singing to them, a song with no words.
The sky was growing pale. Not blue yet. The white before blue.

I filled the trays: wheat, a little broken corn, and a handful of the yellow lentils Laila used for soup, because my father always said a pigeon who eats lentils flies home faster, and I have never been able to prove he was wrong. The grain made a soft hiss as it poured. It is one of the sounds I hear at night, now.

Then I took the telephones out of the cloth bag and set them in their row on the low wall. Eleven of them that day. I have counted them in my head ten thousand times since. A Nokia with no back. There, I thought. You are alive.

“Where you left it.”

The sky was blue now. The sun was not over the ridge yet, but the light was coming, the way the sound of a river comes before you see the river. The high thin buzzing was there, as it was every morning. Going around and around.

I looked up.

Eight.
Seven.
In the east room, the little white shape bent down. Stood up. Held something up in its hand.
It had found it. Whatever it was looking for, it had found it.
Six.
Five.
I did not move my hand again.

The investigators asked me why, twice. The first time I said there wasn’t time, the missile was in its last seconds and couldn’t turn hard enough to follow, which is true. The second time I said I froze, which is also true.
There’s a third answer I never gave them.

I didn’t move my hand again because I was afraid that if I moved it, I’d move it the wrong way. And I knew, the way you know something with your whole body, that every direction was the wrong way. That I was holding a little box of light on the roof of a house where a man was carrying a bird down the stairs toward his daughter, and that wherever I put it, it was going to land on somebody’s morning.
Four.
Three.
Two.
On the screen, the two small white shapes in the east room were very close together. Touching.
One.
TEN · Nasim
I will tell you what I was doing. That is all I can tell you. I was not there for what happened. I was only there for what I was doing.
I was whistling for my birds.

Every kaftar-baz has his own whistle, the way every man has his own walk. Mine is two notes, one high and one low, and then a third that goes up at the end like a question. My birds know it the way a dog knows its name. When they are high and deciding whether to come home or go to another man’s roof, it is the thread that pulls them down.
I put two fingers in my mouth and whistled it. High, low, and the question.
And Uncle came first.

He always came first. He dropped out of the sky like a stone, wings folded, falling and falling until you were sure he had forgotten how to stop, and then, an arm’s length above the roof, the wings opened, clap, and he put his red feet forward and landed on my hand.
On my hand. He did that sometimes. Only on the good days.
He was cold from the sky. I could feel his heart going very fast against my fingers, so fast it was not a beat but a hum. He looked at me with one orange eye.
Is it time?
“You’re early,” I said. “Where are the others? Did you leave them?”
And below me, from the window of the back room, Parisa shouted.
“Baba! I found it!”

That was all. The sandal. The one that had escaped in the night. She had found it under the mattress or behind the sewing machine, and she wanted me to know, because there was nothing that happened to Parisa that she did not want me to know.
“Show me!” I called.
And I turned, with Uncle against my chest, and walked toward the top of the stairs, to look down at the window and see her hold it up.

I want you to understand how small this was. It was the smallest thing I did that day, smaller than the water, smaller than the grain. I turned around on my own roof to see my daughter hold up a pink plastic shoe. I did not decide to do it. My feet did it, the way your feet go to the door when someone you love knocks.
One step. Two steps. Three.
I put my foot on the first stair and looked down, past the edge of the roof, toward the window with its white curtain going in and out.
I saw, through the gap in the curtain, a small hand, holding up something pink, with a yellow flower on it.
I took the second step.

I was thinking about the door. I was thinking: I will fix it today. After the shop, before the tea. I will plane the bottom where it sticks, the way my father showed me, and when Parisa comes home from school I will open it for her and it will swing like a bird’s wing, and she will say, Baba, it doesn’t stick, and I will say, No, jan. Nothing sticks anymore.
I was thinking about that.
I took the third step.
There was no sound.

People ask me about the sound. The neighbors said it was the loudest thing they had ever heard, that it broke windows in the next street. I believe them. But there is no sound in my memory. There is only the rest of it.
There was a light.

Not a flash. More like the light that comes into a room when someone opens a door in the dark, only the door was everywhere, and the light was not coming in. It was coming out. Out of the roof. Out of the bricks under my feet. As if the house my father built had been holding a sun inside it all these years, and had finally let it go.
Then I was lifted.

I do not know another word. I was lifted the way you lift a child, under the arms, very fast, by a hand much bigger than mine. The stairs went away from my feet. Uncle went out of my hands. I felt the small hum of his heart leave my fingers, and I did not see where he went.
I was in the air.

I want to tell you that it was terrible. It was not terrible. That is the thing I have never been able to say to anyone. It was quiet. I was turning, slowly, the way my birds turn, and I saw the sky, very blue now, and the edge of the eastern ridge with the sun just coming over it, the first gold of the day. And I saw, very high, above everything, a glitter. A handful of salt.
My birds. Turning all together. Flashing white.
They were coming home.
Then I was in the mulberry tree.

My mother’s tree, that she planted the year I was born. It caught me. I fell into it from above, and the branches broke under me, crack and crack and crack, leaves in my mouth, the branches holding me and letting me go and holding me and letting me go, the way a mother hands a baby down a staircase, from arm to arm, and then I was on the ground.
On my back. In the courtyard. Under the tree.
And then, at last, I heard something.
I heard the bricks.

I heard them coming down behind me, where the house was. Not all at once. A long slow sound like a man pouring gravel from a sack, and then a stop, and then a little more. Patient. As if the house were deciding, one brick at a time, what to keep and what to let go.
I heard dust. I did not know dust had a sound. It is the sound of a very large thing breathing out.
The dust came down on me like flour. I could not see the house. I could see only white, falling, slowly, slowly, and in the white, very far away, a gold light where the sun was.
I lay in the white, under my mother’s tree, and I thought: Parisa found her sandal.
That is what I thought.

I did not think my house. I did not think my wife. I did not think my daughter. Not yet. The mind does not go there first. The mind is kind, for a little while. It gives you one last small thing to hold before it gives you the big one.
She found it, I thought. Good. Now she can go to school.
ELEVEN · Kayla
“Splash,” the pilot said.
It’s what you say when the missile hits. Like a stone in a pond. Like a kid jumping in a pool.
On the white hot screen, the house disappeared.

It didn’t explode the way you’d think, fire and a fireball, like the movies. In white hot, the place where the missile lands turns into a flower. A white flower, opening. Petals of heat going out in every direction, very fast, and then slowing, and hanging there, and then the dust comes up through it, cold and gray, and covers it, like somebody pulling a sheet over a bed.
The flower opened at 0602 and nineteen seconds, local time.
It opened over the east room.
“Good effects,” the pilot said, the way he said it every time. It means the missile did what missiles do. It’s not a judgment. It’s like saying the oven’s hot.

Then he picked his sandwich up off the paper towel, looked at it, and put it down again without eating it. In two years of sitting next to that man, it was the only time I ever saw him not finish his sandwich.
“BDA,” said the voice in my headset. “Stay on it.”
Battle damage assessment. It means you look at what you did. You don’t get to look away. You keep the camera on it so that somebody up the chain can put a number in a box.
So I stayed on it.
The dust took four minutes and eleven seconds to clear. I’ve timed it since, on the tape. In my memory it’s an hour. In my memory I’m still waiting for it to clear.

The roof was gone on the east side. The east room didn’t have a ceiling anymore. It had the ceiling inside it: mud and timber and brick in a gray mound, and on top, in the daylight camera, pieces of the cage. Wire. Wood. Small light scattered things that I told myself were feathers. On the west side the roof still stood, and the place where he had stood every morning was still there, flat and empty.
In white hot, the mound glowed the way a fire glows after you’ve put it out. Dull and low and even, all the heat of the blast settling into the bricks.
I looked for them.
Forty-one days I had been able to find those two shapes anywhere in that house, through any open window. The camera sees heat through a curtain. It sees a sleeping child through a cotton blanket.
It does not see through a house that has fallen.
The mound glowed the same dull warmth from top to bottom. There was no white. No shape. Just the house, lying on top of the room, keeping its secret.
White means warm, I thought. Warm means alive.
There was nothing on my screen to say it to.
“Squirter,” the MIC said. It’s the word for somebody who gets out of a strike. “In the courtyard. Under the tree.”
I swung the camera.
A white shape on its back under the tree. Moving, the way a turtle moves on its back. An arm. A leg. It rolled over, slowly, and got up on its hands and knees.
“Is that the target?” said the voice.
“Can’t confirm.”
“Selector status?”
A pause, somewhere. Then: “Selector’s dark.”
The eleven little lights were gone. Under the mound.
“Stay on the squirter.”
So I stayed on him.

He crawled. He crawled across the courtyard on his hands and knees, from the tree to the mound, the way you’d crawl across a dark floor looking for something you’d dropped. And when he got there, he dug.

You can see a lot in white hot. You can see the hands get brighter as a man digs, from the work, from the blood. You can see him throw a brick behind him, and another. You can see that his left arm isn’t working right, that it hangs. You can see him dig with one hand.

Then other shapes came through the gap where the blue door had been. Two, then five, then a dozen. Men, women at the edges, kids. The neighbors, a crowd of candles, running to the mound and kneeling down to dig.
“Multiple military-age males approaching,” the MIC said. “Watch them.”
“They’re digging,” I said.
“Watch them.”
So I watched them dig.
It took them nineteen minutes, with their hands.

Here’s something they teach you in the schoolhouse. A body doesn’t go cold fast. It holds its heat for hours. On bare ground, in the cool of the morning, a body is the warmest thing for a mile. But under a roof that’s just been hit by a missile, everything is warm. The bricks, the timbers, the dust. And the camera spreads its colors across whatever’s in front of it, so that when everything is the same temperature, everything is the same gray.

So when the men pulled the last bricks off and lifted them out, the two of them came out the same color as the mound. Not white. Gray. A medium shape wrapped around a little one, so close you couldn’t see where one stopped.
They were still warm. I knew it then. The people holding them would have felt it in their hands, and thought what anyone would think: she’s still warm, maybe.
But on my screen they were the same color as the world.
You couldn’t tell them apart from the dirt.
The white shape that had dug with one hand took the little gray one in its arms and sat down on the ground with it, and rocked it, back and forth, very slowly, the way you’d rock a baby to sleep.
And the little gray one didn’t get any warmer.
I wrote it down. That’s the job. In the small block capitals, so nobody could misread anything:
0621L. 2X PERSONS RECOVERED FROM STRUCTURE, EAST ROOM. NO MOVEMENT. ASSESSED AS 2X CIVCAS. ADULT FEMALE, CHILD.
CIVCAS means civilian casualties. It’s a word. It goes in a box.
And under it, because the voice asked:
SQUIRTER, ADULT MALE, ALIVE. TARGET STATUS UNCONFIRMED.
When the new crew took the chair, the new sensor operator looked at the screen and then at me.
“You good?”
“I’m good.”
She didn’t believe me. She didn’t say anything else. Nobody says anything else. That’s the deal.

I got my phone out of the locker. Two texts. One from the sitter: chicken was amazing!! he ate a pickle lol. One from my mother: a sunrise over Henderson with a Bible verse across it in curly letters.
On the way home I stopped at the Walmart on Craig Road, because we were out of milk.

It was six-forty in the morning and the store was almost empty, and they were playing a song about being young forever. I got the milk. I got Cheerios. And then I walked past the hot case, where the rotisserie chickens sit in their plastic domes under the heat lamps, in rows.
I stopped.

I stood in front of the rotisserie chickens for I don’t know how long. A guy in an apron asked if I needed help, and I said no, and he went away. I just stood there and looked at them, golden, steaming the insides of their little plastic houses. And I thought about how long one would stay warm, if somebody took it out and put it on the counter. And how you could watch it go, if you had the right camera. From white to gray, a little at a time, so slow you’d never see it unless you watched.
I put the basket down on the floor of the Walmart with the milk and the Cheerios in it, and I walked out.
When I got home, Wyatt was at the counter in his dinosaur pajamas, the ones I’d folded the day before, eating toast.
“Mom, you didn’t get milk.”
“I forgot.”
“You always forget.”
“I know, baby.”
I stood in the kitchen with my keys in my hand and I counted him.
One. Big as a lamp. White.

I put my hand on the back of his neck, under his hair, where it’s warmest, and kept it there. “Mom, your hand’s cold.” I kept it there until he wriggled away and said, “Mom, stop,” and went to get dressed for school.
He was warm. He was so warm.

I opened the fridge. The sitter had saved me two of the chicken thighs, under foil. I took one out with my fingers, cold, and stood in the light of the open fridge in my uniform and ate it. I hadn’t eaten in sixteen hours.
And it was good.
That’s the thing I can’t tell anyone. The lemon and the garlic and the salt. It was the best thing I’d eaten all week.
I didn’t cry. I didn’t throw up. I didn’t feel anything at all, except that the chicken was good, and I was hungry, and my son was warm.
That’s the first day. Nobody tells you that, either. The first day, you don’t feel anything.
You just eat the chicken.
TWELVE · Nasim
They let me hold her until the noon prayer.
In our faith, the dead are buried quickly, the same day if it can be done. It is a mercy. It carries the dead into the earth before the house learns to hold the shape of their absence.
At noon the women came and took her from me, gently, the way you take a sleeping child from a man who has fallen asleep holding her.
I did not let go at first.

My cousin Wahid [wa-HEED], who had come running from the other end of town with his shirt on inside out, held my wrists. Not hard. The way you hold the wrists of a drowning man, to help him, not to stop him. Nasim-jan, he said in my ear, she must be washed. Let her be washed.
And I let her go.
I want to tell you how she looked. I have never told anyone, and I want one person to know.

She looked like she was sleeping. That is what people say, and it was true. There was white dust in her hair, in her eyelashes, in the little gap in her front teeth. There was blood at the back of her head, where I did not look. But her face was clean except for the dust, and her mouth was a little open, the way it always was when she slept, as if she were about to say five minutes.
And in her hand was the sandal.
The one she had found. She held it so tightly that the women could not take it out of her fingers, and in the end they did not try. They washed her around it. They wrapped her around it.
Laila was right. She was buried in her sandals. One on her foot and one in her hand.
Laila was holding her when they found them. Wrapped around her, Wahid told me, the way a hand wraps around a stone. Her back was to the falling roof, and Parisa was in the circle of her arms.
She had turned. In the last second she had heard something, or felt a change in the air, the way mothers feel things, and she had turned and put her body between our daughter and the roof.
It did not help.
I want to say that it did. That is what people want to hear. It did not help. The roof was too heavy. The roof was the house my father built, when I carried the water in a tin cup.
But she turned. It was the last thing she did, and it was the right thing, and it did not help, and I am proud of her for it until I die.

They were washed by the women in my cousin’s house, because there was no house of ours anymore, and wrapped in the kafan [ka-FAN], the plain white cloth every one of us goes into the earth in, rich or poor, so that we all go looking the same.
Laila was wrapped in a long one.
Parisa was wrapped in a small one.

I carried her. They tried to stop me, because my left arm was broken and the bone was pushing against the skin where bones should not push. But I carried her in my right arm. She had been too heavy to carry, the night before, when Laila took her down the stairs. Now she weighed nothing. A child in a kafan weighs nothing. It is as if the cloth is empty, and you are only carrying the idea of a child.

We walked to the graveyard on the hill outside the town, where my father is, and my mother. A long line of men in the afternoon heat with the dust still in our hair. The women stayed behind, as is our custom, and their crying followed us up the hill like a wind.
I saw the young man.
The one with the cracked Samsung. The one who laughed with his whole face.

He stood alone at the edge of the graveyard, by the wall, with his clean hands folded in front of him, and watched us lower them into the ground, the long white shape and then the small one. When the first earth went in, he turned and walked away down the hill.
I never saw him again.

I do not know why he came. Maybe because he heard that the man who fixed telephones had lost his family, and he was a polite young man who had once given the girl a sweet. Maybe because he knew exactly why the sky had fallen on my roof, and could not stay away. Maybe both.
His telephone was under my house, under the bricks, with the others. I never went back for it.
The birds came home that evening.
Wahid’s boy came running to tell me. Kaka [KAA-kaa], Uncle Nasim, your birds are back. They are on your house.
So I walked back through the town in the blue hour, with my arm tied against my chest in a scarf.
The blue door lay in the street, blown off its hinges. I stepped over it. It did not stick anymore. Nothing sticks anymore.
And on the edge of the roof that was left, the west side, in a row, were my birds.
Nineteen of them. Three were never found, and Uncle was one of them. I looked for him for weeks. I never found a feather.

But nineteen had come down out of the sky to the roof where they always came, and there was no loft for them, and no man in the middle of the roof to whistle them in. So they had landed on the edge, in a row, where the telephones used to sit, and they were waiting.
They looked down at me with their orange eyes.
Is it time?
I sat down in the courtyard, under what was left of the tree, in the dust, and looked up at them, and they looked down at me.
And above them, high and thin and patient, was the sound.
It had stayed. All day, while we dug, while we washed them, while we carried them up the hill, it had been there, going around and around, watching.
I did not nod to it. I did not say good morning.
I only looked up at it, for the first time in my life, the way it had always believed I was looking. As if I knew exactly what it was.
INTERLUDE TWO · 1907–1923
A Short History of Watching from Above
The Pharmacist’s Pigeons

This is a true story. It is about how seeing from the sky turned into striking from the sky, how quickly it happened, and how the rules meant to protect the people underneath always seem to arrive after the funeral.

In the small German town of Kronberg [KRON-berg], in the hills above Frankfurt, a pharmacist named Julius Neubronner [NOY-bron-er] kept pigeons for his work. They were homing pigeons. A homing pigeon always flies home, however far away you take it. Let one go at a hospital in the next town with a prescription tied to its leg, and it flies straight back to the pharmacy. The birds did not care what they carried. They only wanted to go home.
One day a pigeon was lost in the fog and did not come back for four weeks. Neubronner wondered where it had been. And he had an idea: what if a pigeon could take a picture?

He built a tiny camera of wood and metal, light enough for a bird to carry, with a little clock inside that opened the shutter by itself while the bird was in the air. He strapped it to the bird’s chest with a small harness, like a waistcoat, and let the birds go. When they came home, he had something almost no one had seen before: the world as a bird sees it. Rooftops from above. Streets with tiny people in them who had no idea they were being photographed. At the edge of some pictures, a blurred gray shape: the tip of the bird’s own wing.
He applied for a patent in 1907. People bought the photographs as postcards. They were charmed.

The army saw something else. A camera that could fly over the enemy with no man in it. A spy that could not be questioned if it was caught. When the Great War came, camera pigeons were tried over its battlefields.
Neubronner had only wanted to know where his lost bird had been.
Four years after his patent, in November 1911, Italy was fighting a war in the desert of Libya. Its few new airplanes, flimsy things of wood and cloth, were used at first only to look.

Then one morning a young Italian pilot named Giulio Gavotti [JOO-lee-oh ga-VOT-tee] flew over an enemy camp at an oasis with four small bombs in a leather bag on his lap, not much bigger than oranges. He leaned over the side of his plane and dropped one. It was the first bomb ever dropped from an airplane. That evening he wrote to his father about it. He was excited. He did not know whether he had hit anyone.
Four years. That is how long it took, from a pigeon’s picture of a rooftop to a bomb falling on people who could not see it coming.

After that it went very fast. Within a few years, airplanes and airships were bombing London and Paris, and towns where the people underneath were bakers and seamstresses and children. When that war ended, the governments of the world sent lawyers to The Hague, in Holland, to write rules for war from the air.

In 1923 they wrote them down. Bombing to terrify ordinary people was forbidden. A bomb could only be dropped on a military target. If a pilot could not tell whether a target was military, he must not drop the bomb.
They were good rules, written by serious people who had seen what happened to London.
And no country ever agreed to them. Not one. They were printed and put on a shelf, a promise that nobody made.

What is a rule worth, if no one has to follow it? What is a promise worth, if it comes after the bomb has fallen? And when it comes that late, who is it really for: the people underneath, or the people who need to sleep at night?

Some of Neubronner’s photographs are not like the others. They are tilted, because the bird was turning when the shutter opened, and they show a rooftop very close, rushing up, with the blurred gray tip of a wing at the edge.

Look at one long enough and it becomes a picture of the bird coming home. You can almost see what it saw. The roof, getting bigger. The little door of the loft. The man standing there with grain in his hand. The thing it had flown toward the whole time, through the fog and the cold, with a camera strapped to its chest that it did not understand, taking pictures of a world it did not care about.
It only wanted to go home.
It did not know what it was carrying. It never does.
III. THE FORTIETH DAY
THIRTEEN · Nasim
The envelope came on the twenty-third day.

I counted the days the way grief counts them, which is in nights. Twenty-three times I had lain down on the half of the roof that was left, among the nineteen birds, and closed my eyes, and opened them again, and found that it was still true.
A boy came from the governor’s compound with a paper. The Americans wished to see me. Tomorrow, at ten.
I knew why. By then, in our country, everyone knew someone it had happened to. There were always two things that came after. First the silence. Then the envelope.

I put on my good clothes, the ones I had worn to my wedding, which Wahid’s wife had found in a trunk of things saved from the house. The shirt was too big now. I tied my broken arm in a clean scarf and walked through the bazaar, past my shop. The shutter was down. Someone had written on it in chalk, in a child’s hand, God is great, and under it, in a different hand, the telephone man’s family, and nothing else, as if whoever wrote it had not known how to finish the sentence.

They took me to a room with a long table, plastic chairs, a picture of the President on the wall, and an air conditioner in the window that roared like a lion and made the room as cold as the inside of a well.

There was an American at the table, younger than me, in the tan uniform, with a clean, careful face. He stood up when I came in. That surprised me. He put his hand on his heart, the way we do, and said in bad Dari [da-REE], our language, salaam alaikum [sa-LAAM a-LAY-kum], peace be upon you, which he had clearly learned for this. Beside him sat an interpreter from Kabul with a pen behind his ear.
The American spoke for a long time, and the interpreter put it into Dari. I remember every word. I have the paper still.

The government of the United States was deeply sorry for the loss of my wife and daughter. On the morning of the strike, American forces had believed they were acting against a person who was a threat to the people of Afghanistan and to American soldiers. Afterwards the matter had been looked into carefully, and it had been found that I was not that person. A mistake had been made. A tragic mistake. They wished to express their sympathy.
The interpreter said a tragic mistake in English first, before he said it in Dari, as if he wanted me to hear how the words sounded in their own language.
Then the American took a thick white envelope out of a folder and pushed it across the table to me with two fingers, gently, the way you push a cup of tea toward a guest.
I did not touch it.
The interpreter leaned toward me and said quietly, not translating, just a man talking to a man, “Brother. Open it here. Then they can write that you opened it.”
