It was money. American dollars, new ones, in a paper band. And a sheet of paper, in English and in Dari, with a place at the bottom for a signature.
My hands counted the money before my heart knew what it was holding. I have kept a shop for twenty years. When someone gives you money, your hands count it.
Four thousand dollars.

My hands had counted it into two piles on the table without asking me. Two thousand for Laila. Two thousand for Parisa. Perhaps they meant it as one sum, for the house, for the arm. But there they were. Two piles. One for a woman of thirty-eight who sewed dresses and made up proverbs. One for a girl of eight who counted screws in the lid of a jam jar.
The same size. I remember that the most. Someone had decided that a child was worth the same as her mother. I did not know if that was a kindness or the opposite of one.
The interpreter read me the paper slowly, with his finger under the words, though I can read. I let him. I wanted to hear it in a voice.
The money was a condolence payment, given ex gratia [eks GRAY-shee-uh].
“What does that mean?”
“It is Latin,” he said. “It means from kindness. It means they are not giving it because they have to. They are giving it because they want to.”
The next line said the payment was not an admission of responsibility, and did not mean that the United States owed me anything under any law.
“So it is a gift,” I said.
The interpreter did not answer.
“They kill my wife and my child, and they give me a gift.”

He said something to the American in English. Perhaps he translated me. Perhaps he softened it. The American’s face changed a little, the way a lake changes when a cloud goes over it, and he said something short.
“He says he is very sorry,” the interpreter said. “He says he has a daughter too.”
I signed the paper.
People in America have asked me why, people with kind faces and notebooks, as if a man with a broken arm and no house and no family, in a cold room under a picture of the President, had a choice.

But that is not the real answer. The real answer is that I understood, sitting there, that the paper was not for me. It was for them. It was so that somewhere, in some office far away, a man could put it in a folder and close the folder and say: it is finished. And I thought: let it be finished for them, then. It will never be finished for me. Let somebody have that.
That was my kindness. My ex gratia.
When I stood, the American stood too, and put out his hand. I want to tell you I left it in the air. That would be a better story.
I took it. His hand was cold from the air conditioner, and it held mine a little too long.

I walked out into the heat of the day, which was like stepping into a bath, with four thousand dollars in my good shirt, and I did not know where home was, so I walked to the ruin. And that afternoon I did a thing I am ashamed of, and not ashamed of at all. I went to the bazaar and bought grain. The best grain, wheat and corn and the yellow lentils, more than they could eat in a month, and I carried it up the stairs that were left and poured it out for my birds onto the bricks, a golden hill of it, and sat and watched them eat.
From kindness, I said to them.
They did not care where it came from. They are birds.
FOURTEEN · Kayla
They interviewed me twice.

It’s called a commander-directed investigation. An officer who wasn’t involved asks everybody what happened and writes a report, and a commander decides if anybody did anything wrong. It’s not a court. You sit in a room with a fake plant in the corner and a box of Kleenex nobody touches, and a major you’ve never met asks you questions in a voice like a dentist.

The first time, he had my log, all forty-one days of it, with yellow sticky tabs coming out the side like feathers. He read me the line from day thirty-three, out loud: Subject on roof. Looks up at aircraft at dawn, daily. Possible awareness of surveillance.
“What did you mean by that?”
“I meant he looked up. Every morning.”
“At the aircraft.”
“At the sky.”
“You wrote aircraft.”
“I know what I wrote.”
The second time was a month later. Same plant. Same Kleenex. He slid a printout across the table.
“I thought you should see this before the report goes up,” he said, and it was the only kind thing he ever said to me.
It was what they’d found when they went back and looked at everything again. Not the pieces that made the picture. The pieces we’d walked past. It was written plainly, like a weather report.

The man on the roof was not the facilitator. He was a phone repairman with a shop in the bazaar, with no known connection to any armed group. The phone belonged to a customer who had left it with him for repair several times. He tested phones on the roof because the signal was better there. The visitors were customers and neighbors. The sacks were bird feed. The structure on the roof was a pigeon loft.
The repairman kept pigeons.
He looked up at the sky because he was watching his birds.
“So it was all wrong,” I said.
“It wasn’t all wrong,” the major said. “The selector was real. The phone was there. It just wasn’t his.”
“So we were trying to kill a phone.”

He didn’t answer that. He told me what the report would say, picking his words like a man crossing a creek on stones. The strike was conducted within the rules of engagement. The target was positively identified, based on the information available at the time. The information turned out to be wrong. An error in the final seconds of terminal guidance moved the point of impact. No negligence or misconduct by any individual.
“Terminal guidance,” I said. “That’s me.”
“That’s the system.”
“That’s my hand.”
“That’s the system, Sergeant.”
Here’s the math I did that night, at the kitchen table at four in the morning, with a glass of my mother’s boxed wine and the fan going.
If I’d held the box on him. If I’d been faster than the lag. If the bird hadn’t come down, if the girl hadn’t shouted, if he hadn’t turned.
The missile would have hit him on the roof, alone. The wife and the girl would have been in the east room, outside the circle, alive. Good effects. The pilot would have finished his sandwich.
And the man on the roof would have been a phone repairman who kept pigeons.

You understand? There was no version of that morning where I did my job perfectly and nobody innocent died. The only version where nobody innocent died was the one where the missile never left the rail, and that was decided a long way up, by people reading my log.

So which is it? Is it my fault, because my hand moved the box onto his family? Or not my fault, because if my hand had been perfect I’d have killed an innocent man instead, and that would have been the system working? Is a perfect shot at the wrong man better or worse than a bad one? Is one dead innocent better than two?
I sat at the table till the sky went gray and couldn’t answer it. I’ve thought about it every day for three years. I still can’t tell you which one I would rather have done.

Something else I found out later. In 2013 the President put out a rule for strikes like ours. Before a lethal strike there had to be near certainty the target was there, and near certainty no civilians would be hurt. The White House called it the highest standard it could set. I remember feeling proud of it, in tech school.

What I didn’t know was that it only applied outside what they called areas of active hostilities. Afghanistan was an area of active hostilities. So in the real war, the rule didn’t apply. Not to us. Not to the house in Maidan Shahr.

I read that on my phone in a Starbucks two years too late. I’m not saying it would have saved them. Maybe no rule in the world would have caught the pigeons. But it would have been nice to know the highest standard we could set had been set.
The pilot didn’t sit at any kitchen table at four in the morning. I want to be fair to him. He’s not a villain in this. Nobody is. That’s the whole problem.
I asked him the week after the second interview, in the box, at three in the morning, watching a road in Helmand [hel-MAND] where nothing was happening.
“Do you think about it.”
He chewed for a while. “Sure.”
“How do you sleep.”
He was an honest man. He gave it real thought.
“Kayla. We did everything right. The process worked. The inputs were bad. That’s on whoever built the picture. If you start carrying the inputs, you’ll never put anything down again.”
“I built the picture.”
“You fed it. Lots of people fed it. Twenty people read that line and signed off. You think you’re the only one who should’ve caught it?” He shook his head. “That’s ego. Thinking it’s all yours.”

Then he told me he’d taken his girls to Lake Mead on Saturday, and Lacey had caught an eleven-pound striped bass and screamed the whole time she was reeling it in. He smiled, a real smile. “Bring Wyatt out sometime.”

And I thought: he’s not pretending. He really did watch his daughter scream with joy at an eleven-pound fish, and it really was wonderful, and he really did kill a woman and a child in Maidan Shahr six weeks before. He holds both. It doesn’t break him.
And I could not tell you which one of us was the sick one.

The base had a psychologist with an office right in the building. The Air Force had surveyed about a thousand of us, I found out later. Most were fine. Proud of the work, proud of protecting the guys on the ground. A small number had real post-traumatic stress. A lot more were just burned out, from the nights and the twelve-hour shifts and living two lives.
She gave me a form with seventeen questions. Repeated, disturbing memories. Trouble falling asleep. Feeling cut off from other people. I gave myself mostly twos. A little bit.
She looked at the form and then at me.

“There’s a term we use now. Moral injury.” She put the form down. “Post-traumatic stress is usually about fear. But you were never in danger. Nobody shot at you. Moral injury is when you do something, or fail to stop something, that goes against what you believe is right. It’s not that you’re scared. It’s that you can’t make it fit with who you thought you were.”
“So what’s the treatment,” I said.
She was quiet for a second.
“We’re still working on that.”
FIFTEEN · Nasim
On the fortieth day, we did the chehlom [CHEH-lum].

In our tradition, the first forty days after a death are the days of mourning. People come to sit with you. The Holy Book is read through, all of it, by men who come in turns. And on the fortieth day everyone gathers one last time, and there is food, and prayer, and then, they say, the first part of the grief is over. The soul has gone on. The family can begin to live again.
That is what they say.
I will tell it slowly, because it was slow. It was the longest day of my life. The day of the strike was a moment. The fortieth day was a mountain.
I woke on the roof before dawn, as I always did.

The birds lived in the open now, on the half of the roof that was left, under a sheet of blue plastic stretched between two broken timbers. I had not built them a new loft. I did not have it in me. They slept in a row along the edge, where the telephones had been.
I lay there and listened to them, and did not open my eyes.

That is the first thing about grief that no one tells you. The waking. Every morning, for one moment, you do not remember. Your body wakes before your memory does, and your body is happy. It is warm, it has slept, the birds are talking. For half a breath you are the man you were. And then your memory comes into the room and sits down on your chest.
Every morning. Forty mornings. It never once failed to come.
I went down the stairs that were left.

Wahid’s wife and the women of the street had swept the courtyard every day since, as if dust could be made to understand it was not welcome. The mulberry tree had been cut back where its branches were broken. It looked like a man with his sleeves rolled up.
And here is what I did. I want to tell you exactly.
Wahid had set up a small gas ring for me on a stone. I lit it, and boiled the kettle, and made green tea.
And I set out three cups.

I did not decide to. My hands did it. They took three small glass cups from the shelf and set them on the tray in a row, the way they had every morning for eight years. One for me, one for Laila, and a small one for Parisa, with only a little tea and a lot of sugar. I poured the tea into all three, and sat down on the step, and looked at the tray.
Three cups.
Two of them going cold.

I did that every morning. Forty mornings. Wahid’s wife saw me do it once and said nothing, and the next day she brought a fresh packet of sugar and set it beside the tray and went away. She understood. Some things you cannot stop your hands from doing. You can only make sure there is sugar.
The men came at nine to read.

They came through the gap where the blue door had been. Old men from the mosque, young men from the bazaar, men I had fixed radios for. They sat on carpets in the shade of the cut-back tree and took the Holy Book in turns, reading in the old language in a low voice that rose and fell like water over stones.
I sat with them. I could not read. My mouth would not make the words.
And while they read, I heard her.

I want to be careful telling you this. I am not a madman. I am a man who fixes radios. I know the difference between a sound and a memory. But there are things in grief that are neither. You can decide what to call them.
The first was the stairs.

In the middle of a verse, I heard someone coming up the outside stairs. Slap. Slap. Slap. Small feet. Plastic sandals on cold brick. Slow, the way she came up in the mornings when she was still sleepy.
I turned my head.
There was no one on the stairs.

I knew there was no one before I turned. I turned anyway. It is not that you believe she is there. It is that some part of you older than believing, a part that was built to listen for her and has never been told to stop, turns your head for you. And you let it. Because the alternative is to tell that part of you it can stop listening, and you will not. You would rather turn your head a thousand times to an empty staircase than once tell yourself you do not need to.
I turned my head eleven times that morning. I counted, after.

At noon the women brought the food. Rice with raisins and carrots, and the halwa [HAL-wa], the sweet of flour and butter and sugar that is always made for the dead, because the old women say the dead are hungry for sweetness, and the smell reaches them. The whole courtyard smelled of butter and cardamom. It was the smell of every funeral of my life, and every wedding, because they are the same smell.
I sat with a plate on my knees and did not eat.
And Laila said, quite clearly, in my ear: Nasim. Eat something. You look like a broom.

That was the second thing. Her voice. Not a whisper from the grave. Her ordinary voice, the one she used in the kitchen, a little impatient, a little amused. It was a thing she said, when I was thin from a fever, or worked too late at the shop.
I knew it was my own mind, holding her voice the way you turn a coin over in your pocket because it is the only one you have left.
I ate a spoonful of rice.
Good, she said.

And I put the spoon down and put my face in my good hand, and the men around me went quiet, and an old man I did not know put his hand on the back of my neck and kept it there, very still, while I made a sound I had not made since I was a child.

In the afternoon the mullah [MUL-la], the man who leads the prayers at our mosque, said what is said. That a child who dies before she is grown goes straight to Paradise and waits at the gate for her parents, to take them by the hand and lead them in. He said Parisa would be the first face I saw.
People wept. It is a beautiful thing to say. It has been said in our country for a thousand years, at the graves of a thousand thousand children.
I sat and listened, and I thought: she will be waiting in her sandals.
That was all I could think. Both of them. One on her foot and one in her hand. She will hold it up when she sees me at the gate, and say, Baba, I found it.
And I will not be able to say show me. Because I will already have seen.
By evening everyone had gone. Wahid embraced me at the gap where the door had been and said, Sleep at my house tonight, at least tonight, and I said no.
It was the fortieth night. They say that for forty days the soul stays near the people it loved, and on the fortieth night it rises and goes on.
I lay down on the half of the roof that was left, under the stars, among my birds.
And the sound was there.

It had never gone away. I do not know if it was the same one, or if the people who fly them go home at night. I only know it had watched every one of the forty days. It had watched us dig, and wash them, and carry them up the hill. It had watched me set out three cups every morning. It had watched me turn my head to the empty stairs eleven times.
It knew more about my grief than anyone.
That night I dreamed for the first time since the strike.
I was on the roof, the whole roof, the way it was. The loft was there, with Uncle in it. It was dawn, the color that has no name.

And Laila came up the stairs with Parisa behind her in her sandals, and they stood at the top of the stairs, at the place where I had stood when the light came out of the bricks. They were not hurt. They were exactly as they were. Laila had flour on her hands. Parisa had sleep in her eyes.
“Nasim,” Laila said, “come down. Breakfast is ready.”
“Come down, Baba. The tea’s getting cold.”
“In a minute,” I said. “I am waiting for the birds.”
Laila smiled at me the way she smiled when I was being a kaftar-baz, the smile that meant she knew exactly what I was and had decided to love it anyway.
“They’ll come home,” she said. “They always come home. Come and eat.”
“In a minute,” I said.
And they turned and went down the stairs, slap, slap, slap, and I heard the door stick and then give, and I heard Laila set the cups on the tray, one, two, three.
And I stood on the roof and looked up at the sky, waiting for my birds.
And I did not go down.
I woke with my face wet and the stars going out.
This is the part I have never told anyone. Not Wahid. Not the doctor with the soft voice who asked me, years later, in a small white room, whether I ever thought about hurting myself.

When I woke, I was angry. Not at the Americans. Not at God. At myself, in the dream, for saying in a minute. They had come up the stairs to fetch me, with flour on their hands, and I had stayed on the roof to wait for birds.

And then I understood that it was not a dream about them. It was a dream about what I did every morning for eight years. Every morning they called me down to breakfast, and every morning I said in a minute, and stayed on the roof with my face turned up.
That was why I was on the roof. That was why I was alive.
Because I was a kaftar-baz. A man who looked at the sky when he should have been looking at his family.
And they were in the house, where a man should be.
SIXTEEN · Kayla
It started with the coffee.
About three weeks after the strike, I was on shift, and I’d put a big 7-Eleven coffee on the console next to the joystick and forgotten it. Around two in the morning I looked down at it.
And I saw it cooling.

Not oh, my coffee’s cold. I saw it. I looked at the paper cup and saw the heat in it, a bright white disc at the top, a thin wavering thread of white rising out of the hole in the lid, and the whole thing, so slowly you’d never see it if you looked away, getting dimmer. White to a little less white. A little less white to the gray of a cloud.

I sat there for forty minutes watching a cup of coffee cool. The pilot said something to me twice and I didn’t hear him. When I finally drank it, it tasted like nothing, and I thought: there. It’s dead now.
That’s when I knew something was wrong with me.

I’m not telling you I got superpowers. My eyes are regular eyes. I’m telling you that after two years of twelve-hour nights looking at a world made of heat, and then that morning, and then the nineteen minutes, my brain started doing it on its own. Like when you play Tetris too long and close your eyes and the blocks keep falling. Your brain learns a way of seeing, and then it won’t let go.
Mine learned heat.

It got worse the way water gets into a basement. At the grocery store I’d look at the cashier’s hands going back and forth over the scanner and see two little lamps. The people behind me in line, a string of candles, like a procession.

I stopped buying hot food. It sounds like nothing. I stopped going to Panda Express, which Wyatt loved, because I couldn’t sit there with the orange chicken steaming on the plate and know I’d watch it go from white to gray the whole meal and not taste any of it. I ate cold things. Salads. Yogurt. I lost eleven pounds. My mother said I looked good.
And at night.
Every night I wasn’t on shift, I went into Wyatt’s room and stood in the doorway with the hall light behind me, and I counted him.
One. A white shape under the rocket-ship blanket. A big lamp. Warm.
And I’d stand there and watch to make sure he stayed white.

That’s the part I can’t explain to anyone who hasn’t done the job. I could hear him breathing. I could see his chest go up and down. But the part of me that sat in the box for two years didn’t trust breathing. It trusted only heat. So I’d stand in the doorway long enough to be sure he wasn’t fading, and that if he was, I’d see it. Some nights an hour.

One night that winter he had a fever. A hundred and two. He was hot as a stove. And I stood in his doorway at four in the morning and couldn’t tell if he was too hot or just hot. My brain kept saying white means warm, warm means alive, and he was the warmest he’d ever been, and some broken part of me looked at him burning up in his little bed and thought: good. He’s so alive.
I didn’t give him Tylenol till six. I sat in the doorway till six, watching him glow, because he looked so alive.
The fever broke on its own. He was fine. He was always fine.
I’ve never told anyone that. That’s the worst thing in this book that I did on purpose.

I lasted another year and a half like that, counting him. Then, in the spring of 2021, I put in my papers. Nobody tried very hard to stop me. My record was clean. The investigation had found no misconduct. On paper I was exactly what I’d been before.

The pilot gave me a card his wife had picked out, a sunset with Wishing You Peace on Your Journey in gold letters. Inside he’d written: An honor to fly with you. Lake Mead invitation stands. Bring the kid. It’s in a drawer.
On the drive home from the base for the last time, the sun was in front of me and the desert was the color of a lion, and I thought: that’s it. You’re out.
And I thought: you’re never out.
A month later I got a job in the surveillance room of a casino on the Strip. Watching cameras. Night shift. It was the only thing I knew how to do.
SEVENTEEN · Nasim
After the fortieth day, I went back to the shop, because Wahid’s wife told me, gently, that a man who does not work will soon be dead or mad, and I had not decided yet which I wanted to be.

The people came slowly. They brought me their broken telephones and did not look me in the eye, and then, after a few weeks, they did. They talked about the price of flour and whose son was getting married. They did not talk about the roof. It was as if the whole town had agreed, without speaking, to give me the gift of an ordinary day.
I fixed telephones. I did not take them home anymore.
The two years after are not a story. They are only time.

I lived in the two rooms on the west side that still stood, behind a new tin door that does not stick. I built the birds a small loft on the half of the roof that was left and flew them every morning. I had told myself I would stop. I could not. My body went up the stairs at dawn the way it always had. But I did not look up at the sound anymore. When it was there, I looked at the birds.

The war came closer. The men in the trucks with the white flags came down out of the mountains into the valleys, and then into the towns. The Americans were leaving; they had made an agreement with the men in the trucks. Everyone knew how it would end. No one said it. It was like the sound in the sky.
I did not care who won. I had nothing left for either side to take.
In the middle of August 2021, Maidan Shahr fell.

It was not dramatic. There was some shooting at night. In the morning the soldiers on the walls of the governor’s compound were gone, and different men sat on the walls with their legs over the edge, with long hair and white flags and Kalashnikovs, eating apricots. The town woke up and belonged to someone else. By evening, Kabul had fallen too.
That afternoon, my telephone rang.

A foreign woman, with an interpreter on the line. She worked for an organization that kept records of civilians harmed in the war. Because the Americans had admitted the strike was a mistake, my name was on a list of people they had agreed to help leave the country.
“Why?” I said.
“She says it is part of making amends,” the interpreter said. “Making it right.”
I looked out at the street, where a boy with a Kalashnikov taller than he was stood eating a melon and spitting the seeds into the gutter.
“How do you make it right?” I said.
The interpreter did not translate that. He said, “Brother. Do you want to go or not? There is not much time.”

I did not think about it long. My wife and daughter were on the hill, and would be on the hill whether I was in Maidan Shahr or on the moon. And the men on the walls were the same men who, the last time they ruled, had banned the flying of pigeons, saying it wasted time and took a man’s eyes from God. They went from roof to roof, opening the lofts and killing the birds. I was young then. I hid three of my father’s best birds in a crate in the cellar for five years and fed them by candlelight.
I did not think I had five more years of candlelight in me.
“Yes,” I said.
The night before I left, I let the birds go.

You cannot take nineteen birds through an airport with men with guns at every gate. So I opened the loft in the dark, which you must never do, and took them out one by one, and held each one against my chest a moment and felt the hum of its heart, and threw it up into the night. They did not understand. Birds do not fly in the dark. They fluttered up and came down again, confused, on the wall, on the cut-back tree, and sat there and looked at me. Is it time?
All but one.

A young gray bird with a white collar, the son of Uncle, hatched in the loft the spring before the strike. I had not been able to name him. But he had Uncle’s collar and Uncle’s orange eye, and Uncle’s way of landing on my hand on the good days.

I put him in a shoebox, from a pair of school shoes I had bought for Parisa in Kabul, which she never wore because she would only wear her sandals. I cut holes in the lid with my father’s soldering iron and put a little grain in the corner.
In the morning I walked out of Maidan Shahr in my good shirt, the one I was married in, with the shoebox under my good arm and nothing else.

The airport was hell. You have seen it. Everyone saw it. The crowds at the gates. The sewage canal where people stood to their waists in filth, holding up their papers. The children passed over the walls from hand to hand. The young men who held onto the wheels of the airplane as it took off, and fell.

I was there for three days. I stood in the canal with the shoebox held over my head and my papers in my teeth. When people pushed, I held it higher. Sometimes I felt a small shift of weight, a scratch of claws on cardboard. That was how I knew he was still alive.
On the third day a young American soldier with a sunburned face found my name on his list and waved me through.
Then he saw the box.
“What’s in that?”
“A pigeon.”
He looked at me. He looked at the crowd behind me, the thousands, the dust, the children being handed over the wall.
“Sir, I can’t let you take a live animal on the plane. I’m sorry. You have to leave it.”
I stood at the gate of Kabul airport with the shoebox in my hands.
I had carried it three days through hell. It was the last thing in the world that was mine, that knew my whistle, that would land on my hand.
So I opened the lid.
The bird looked up at me with Uncle’s orange eye, dusty and thin and frightened.
Is it time?
“Yes,” I said. “It’s time.”
I held him against my chest and felt the hum of his heart, and threw him up, high, over the gate and the wire and the crowds, into the hot white sky over Kabul.

He went up in a circle, wider and higher, the way they do. He circled the airport once, twice, a small gray flicker in the white. And I stood at the gate with the empty box and my head back, the way I have stood every morning of my life, and watched him.
And then he turned.
He turned west. Toward the mountains. Toward Wardak, and a town called Maidan Shahr, an hour away if the road is good, and a ruined house with half a roof and a loft made of fruit crates.
He was going home.
A homing pigeon always goes home. It does not matter how far you take it, or what has happened there, or that there is no one left to whistle it down. It goes home.
I watched him until he was a grain of salt.
Then the soldier touched my arm, gently. “Sir. You have to go.”
I got on the airplane with an empty shoebox. I have it still. It is the only thing I brought from my country. Inside, in the corner, there is a little grain, and a single gray feather.
EIGHTEEN · Kayla
I watched it on TV like everybody else.

August 2021. I worked nights at the casino by then, so I watched in the mornings, on the couch, with the sound low so I wouldn’t wake Wyatt, who was nine now. The crowds at the airport. The canal. The C-17 taking off with people running alongside it, and the dots falling off it into the air.
I watched it the way I used to watch the house. Zoomed in. Looking for one man.

I knew it was stupid. There were a hundred thousand people at that airport and I had never seen his face. Only the top of his head, and his shoulders, the right one a little lower than the left, and the way he walked. But I looked. Every crowd shot. Every face in the canal.
I never saw him. I didn’t expect to. I just couldn’t stop looking.
On the twenty-sixth of August, a suicide bomber blew himself up at an airport gate. Thirteen American service members died, and more than a hundred and seventy Afghans.

Three days later, on the twenty-ninth, the United States launched one last drone strike before the last plane left. In Kabul. On a white car in a courtyard. They said it was full of explosives. A righteous strike, someone called it.
Two weeks later the New York Times went to the house.

The man in the car was an aid worker for an American charity. He’d spent the day driving around Kabul, picking up colleagues and filling water containers, because the water was out in his neighborhood. The things they’d watched him load into the car were water jugs. When he pulled into his courtyard at the end of the day, the children of his family ran out to meet him and climbed in to ride the last few feet, the way kids do.
Ten people died. Seven of them were children.

The Pentagon called it a tragic mistake. The Air Force inspector general said it was caused by execution errors, by people reading information in a way that supported what they already believed, and by people not talking to each other. Nobody broke any law. Nobody was negligent. In December, the Secretary of Defense decided no one would be punished. They offered the family condolence payments, and help to leave Afghanistan.
I read every article, at four in the morning in the casino break room, with the slot machines dinging through the wall like a thousand tiny church bells.
Confirmation bias.
I read those two words twenty times. And I wrote down the name of a reporter who had covered it, a woman at a newspaper in New York. I didn’t know yet what I’d do with it.

That was me. That was my log. That was the pigeons going into the picture, and the sacks, and the phones on the wall, and the man looking up. The same mistake, two years later, in a different city, with different people in the box. It wasn’t a new mistake. It was the mistake the system was built to make.
And again nobody was punished.
At least the family is going to get out, I thought.
And then I thought about the house in Maidan Shahr. About whether anybody had put his name on a list.
And I thought: if they did, where would they send him?

The pilot texted me that week. Brutal what’s happening over there. Glad we’re out of it. And a minute later: Lacey made the varsity softball team, with a picture of a girl in a uniform, grinning, holding a bat. She had his smile.
I typed: Congrats to her. I deleted it.
I typed: Do you ever think about the girl in the east room.
I deleted that too.

I put the phone face down and went back to my chair in the surveillance room, where forty screens showed forty views of the casino floor, and a thousand people, in black and white, pulled a thousand levers and waited for something to come down.
INTERLUDE THREE · 1937–1977
A Short History of Watching from Above
Who Counts as a Civilian

This is a true story. It is about the long effort, after the bombing of cities, to write down who must not be killed in war, and how many deaths are too many. It is about the two rules that should have protected the house in Maidan Shahr, and what those rules actually say.

On a Monday afternoon in April 1937, it was market day in the small Basque town of Guernica [ger-NEE-ka], in northern Spain. Spain was at war with itself, and the general on one side had friends in Germany and Italy who wanted to try out their new airplanes.

At about half past four, the bombers came. They came in waves for more than three hours: heavy bombs to knock the buildings down, then fire bombs to burn the ruins, then fighters flying low to shoot the people running into the fields. Most of Guernica was destroyed. How many died is still argued about. The town had almost no soldiers in it at all.

What made Guernica different was that the world saw it. Reporters walked through the ruins the next morning and wrote about it for London and New York. A Spanish painter in Paris painted it in black and white and gray: a screaming horse, a mother holding a dead child, a light bulb like an eye. For the first time, ordinary people far away understood what it meant that a town of people who were fighting no one could be killed by men they never saw, who flew home afterwards and ate dinner.

Then came the Second World War, and Guernica was only the beginning. Every side bombed cities, on purpose: Warsaw, London, Hamburg, Dresden, Tokyo, and at the end two Japanese cities, each destroyed by a single bomb. Tens of millions died, a great many of them in their own houses, under their own roofs.

After that, the world tried again to write rules. It took until 1977. That year the nations agreed to add new rules to the Geneva Conventions, and two of them are the ones that matter for this book. Kayla was taught them in the schoolhouse. They are simple to say and very hard to do.

The first is distinction. In war, you must always tell soldiers from civilians. You may attack soldiers and the things an army fights with. You may not attack people who are not fighting, or their homes, schools and markets. And if you are not sure whether a person is a soldier or a civilian, you must treat them as a civilian.

The second is proportionality. Even when you attack a real military target, you must think about the ordinary people nearby. If the harm to them would be excessive, too much compared with what you expect to gain, you must not attack.
Excessive. The whole rule rests on that word.

It does not say you may never kill a civilian. It says you may not kill too many, compared with what you gain. It is a pair of scales, with the people who might die on one side and the value of the target on the other, and some officer in some room has to weigh them. How much is a facilitator’s phone worth? How many sleeping people in an east room are too many? Is one? Is two?
The rule does not say. It cannot. It leaves that to the people with their hands on the scales.

The United States signed those 1977 rules, but it never ratified them, which means it never made them binding through its own government. Yet it says it follows distinction and proportionality anyway, because they are older than any treaty, and its military teaches them, and its lawyers check strikes against them.
So the rules that should have protected Laila and Parisa were there. They were taught. They were followed. The strike that killed them was checked against them, and found to be within them.
A mistake, they said. Not a crime.

On the day after the bombing of Guernica, a woman sat in the ashes of what had been her house. Nobody wrote down her name. There were too many like her. She sat with her arms around her knees and did not cry, and did not move when the men came with carts for the dead.
Nobody asked her whether her loss had been proportional. Nobody brought her a pair of scales and asked her to weigh her children against a bridge, or a road, or a phone.
Forty years later, careful people in a beautiful room in Geneva argued for years over one word. They found it, and wrote it down, and it has saved lives.
But not one of them went to Guernica and asked the woman in the ashes what it should be.
The law had found a word for how much grief was allowed.
It never asked the grieving.
IV. DESERT INN
NINETEEN · Nasim
In America, the first thing they gave me was a bracelet.

A white paper bracelet with a number on it, which a woman in a uniform put around my wrist on the airplane in Qatar, the way they put a bracelet on a newborn so that nobody takes the wrong baby home. I wore it for two months. I did not take it off to wash. I was afraid that if I took it off, I would no longer be anyone.

They flew us to a military base in the desert of New Mexico, a place called Holloman [HOL-o-man], and put us in great white tents in rows, with cots in rows, and on every folded gray blanket a small bag with a toothbrush and a comb. An old man from Logar [lo-GAR], a province south of Kabul, sat on the next cot with one eye clouded white. They are very organized, he said. They are always very organized. We both understood what he meant, and neither of us said it.
Two months of waiting. The nights were cold and the stars were very close, and I lay on my cot and listened.

There was no sound in that sky. No buzzing. No patient going around and around. I did not sleep well without it. That is a strange thing to tell you, and it is true. For two years I had slept under the sound. Now the silence was too big, and I lay awake in it like a man who has lived beside a river all his life and moves to the desert and cannot sleep for the quiet.
In the autumn a woman with a lanyard full of keys came to the tent and said I was going to a city called Las Vegas. Jobs, she said. Hotels. Casinos.
“What is a casino?”
“A house of gambling,” the interpreter said in Dari. “Very big. They play cards for money. It is lit up all night like a wedding.”
The man from Logar laughed from his cot. “They are sending you to hell, Nasim. At least it will be warm.”

Las Vegas is a city in a desert valley with mountains on every side, like Maidan Shahr, and that is the only way it is like Maidan Shahr. Where we had mud brick, they had glass. Where we had one tap in the courtyard that coughed, they had fountains that danced to music in front of the hotels, throwing water into the air in the middle of the desert all night, as if water were nothing.

They found me two rooms on the second floor of a long low building near a road called Boulder Highway, with carpet the color of mud and a window that looked at a parking lot. The building had a flat roof and a metal ladder up the back, with a padlock that did not lock.
I put my empty shoebox on the shelf. That was my house.
They found me a job, at night, at a casino on the Strip called the Caravanserai [ka-ra-VAN-sa-rye].
When I heard the name, I laughed, and the woman with the keys did not understand why.

Karvansara [kaar-waan-SA-raa] is our word. It is the old word, in all the languages of the road, for the inns that stood a day’s walk apart along the deserts of the Silk Road: a square courtyard with a well in the middle, rooms around the edge, and a great gate that closed at sunset. My father once took me to the ruin of one outside our valley and showed me where the camels knelt. Here, Nasim, he said, every stranger was safe for one night. That was the law of the road.
A desert inn. A house in the desert where strangers sleep.
In America, a desert inn is a house of gambling with a fountain in front of it.
I took the job.

I was a porter. They gave me black trousers, a gray shirt with CARAVANSERAI stitched over the heart in gold thread, a badge with my name in English letters, N-A-S-I-M, which I learned to recognize like a face, and a gray cart with a mop and a bucket and a long stick with a claw for picking things up off the floor. From ten at night until six in the morning I cleaned the casino floor. Spilled drinks. Cigarette ends. The little paper slips the machines give out, which people drop everywhere, like leaves.
And I learned the casino the way I had learned my roof.

It is a great dark room the size of a village, with no windows and no clocks. You cannot tell whether it is day or night. It is always the same light inside, low and gold and red, like the inside of a lamp. And in the room are thousands of machines in rows, like the cots at Holloman, like graves, each one with a bright screen and a stool, and on many of the stools, all night long, a person sits and touches the screen, and the machine makes music.

The noise of it. Thousands of machines, each making its own small song, all at once, forever. At first it made my head ache. After a month I stopped hearing it. After two months I heard it again, differently.
It sounded like birds.
A great loft of birds, thousands of them, all talking in their chests at once. Is it time? Is it time? Is it time?
And in the ceiling were the eyes.

I noticed them the first night. You could not miss them, if you were a man who has spent his life looking up. Every few meters, in rows, black glass domes, like the eyes of great insects, like drops of black oil hanging upside down.
“What are those?” I asked the man who trained me, a big quiet Honduran named Esteban [es-TAY-ban], who had been a porter for nineteen years.

He looked up and smiled with half his mouth. “The eye in the sky. Cameras, in every one. They can read the time on your watch from up there. Don’t steal nothing, hermano.” Hermano [er-MAA-no] is Spanish for brother.
The eye in the sky. Everyone in the casino says it, with a little smile, the way you would speak of a strict old aunt watching from her window.
I stood under the black dome with my mop in my hands and looked up at it for a long time.
“Hey. Nasim,” Esteban said. “Don’t stare at it, man. They don’t like it when you stare.”
TWENTY · Kayla
The surveillance room at the Caravanserai is a box.

Of course it is. I went from one box to another. It’s on the second floor at the end of a hallway the guests never see: dark and cold, a wall of forty screens, a desk with joysticks, the air conditioning set to meat-locker. On the inside of the door there’s a sign that says WHAT YOU SEE HERE STAYS HERE. I laughed out loud the first time I saw it.

The cameras are in the ceiling, hundreds of them, hidden in black glass domes so nobody on the floor can tell which way they’re pointing. Some you can swing and zoom until you can read the serial number on a hundred-dollar bill in a man’s wallet. The guests call it the eye in the sky. So do we. It’s the oldest name in the business.
The job is to watch. The dealers, the players, the cash cage. You learn what normal looks like, and you look for the thing that doesn’t fit.
They hired me in about five minutes. The head of surveillance read sensor operator, MQ-9, four thousand hours on my résumé and looked at me like I was a gift from God.

I was good at it. In three months I caught two dealers skimming chips and a man who’d been switching dice at the craps tables for six weeks. I found him because he did one thing the same way every time. He scratched his left ear before he threw. Just a habit. Like a man looking up at the sky.
The porters come on at ten. You learn them without trying. The big Honduran who hums to himself. The two sisters who work as a pair and never stop talking. They’re part of normal.

I’d been there seven months when a new one started. I didn’t notice him the first night, or the second. The third night I was swinging a camera along the main aisle, and the new porter pushed his cart across the edge of my frame.
And I knew him.

I never saw his face in forty-one days. I saw the top of his head from three miles up. But I saw him walk, hundreds of times. And there’s a thing they teach you in intelligence, and it’s real: you can know a person by their walk better than by their face. A face changes. A walk almost never does. The length of the step, the swing of the arms, which way you lean. It’s a fingerprint you carry in your whole body.

His right shoulder was lower than his left. And his left arm didn’t swing all the way, because his left arm, and I was the only one in America who knew it, had been broken in a fall from a roof into a mulberry tree and had not been set right.
I sat very still in my chair.
And then he stopped under one of the black domes, and he looked up.
Straight up into my camera. Into me.
His face was turned up.
I zoomed in. I couldn’t help it. His face filled my screen, and it was the first time I’d ever seen it.

I think I expected to know it, after forty-one days, the way you know your own mother’s face. I didn’t. It was a stranger’s face. A man in his forties, thin, with a short gray beard, deep lines around the eyes, and a pale hook-shaped scar on his forehead. Tired eyes. The face of a man who’d been awake a long time.

He couldn’t see me. He was looking at a black glass bubble in a ceiling, like a man looking at a strange bird. But his face was turned up, and I was looking down at it, and for a second and a half it felt like he’d already seen me and I was only now seeing him seeing me.
Then the big Honduran said something, and the new porter looked down and pushed his cart away.
Every employee has a file. I found his in a minute.
NAZARI, NASIM. Porter, graveyard. Start date three days ago.
Under notes, somebody in HR had typed: Refugee placement. Limited English. Very polite.
I looked at that name for a long time. Very polite.

I didn’t tell anybody. Who would I tell? Hey, that new porter, I killed his family. He hadn’t done anything. I went home at six and stood in Wyatt’s doorway and counted him, and he was nine and too old for that and I did it anyway, and then I lay in the dark and didn’t sleep.
And the next night, at ten, when the porters came on, I swung a camera to the employee entrance and waited for him.
I followed him every night. I want that on the record, with the rest.

In between the dealers and the drunks, I kept one camera on him, always. I learned his route. Which aisles he did first. What he ate on his break: flatbread from a plastic bag, a cucumber, tea from a thermos. That he prayed on a folded mat in the one corner of the locker room with no camera, and came out with his face calm. That at six he took the bus east, out Boulder Highway. And that every night, at around three in the morning, he stopped under the same dome, by the main aisle, and looked up at it for a few seconds before he went on.
I was building his pattern again.

I knew exactly what I was doing. I’d sit in that cold box at four in the morning watching him mop a floor under the gold lights, and I’d think: you’re doing it again, you sick fuck. You’re building his day.
And I couldn’t stop.

That’s the thing nobody tells you about watching. It’s not the killing that gets into you. The killing is a second. The watching is a life. You watch somebody that long, they become your show. Your house. And you can’t stop, because if you stop, you’ll have to look at what you did instead of at him.
TWENTY-ONE · Nasim
The man came on a Tuesday morning, at the bus stop.

I remember it was Tuesday because the bus was always late on Tuesdays. I was standing on Las Vegas Boulevard at six in the morning in my gray shirt, with my thermos in a plastic bag. The sky was getting light behind the hotels, and their glass was turning the color of fire. On the curb a woman in a gold dress sat with her shoes in her hand, crying very quietly.
A man sat down beside me on the bench.
An American of perhaps fifty. Ordinary, the way a gray stone is ordinary. Gray hair, a gray jacket buttoned against the cold, brown shoes. A face you would forget while you were still looking at it.
He sat for a minute without speaking. Then he said, in Dari, in the Dari of Kabul with the soft r:
“Good morning, Nasim-jan. How are your birds?”

I did not answer for a long time. It was not fear. I had been past fear for two years. It was hearing my own country’s way of speaking in a stranger’s mouth, at a bus stop in Las Vegas. It was like hearing my mother’s voice come out of someone else’s radio.
“I have no birds,” I said. It was not true. I do not know why I said it.
“I’m sorry to hear that. You were a kaftar-baz, weren’t you? I heard you had a fine flock.”
“Who are you?”

He smiled, politely, a smile that did not use the eyes. “I work for an office in Washington. It doesn’t matter which. I learned my Dari in Kabul, a long time ago. I loved your country. People don’t believe that, but I did.”
“What do you want?”
“I don’t want anything. I came to give you something.”
He took a thick white envelope out of his jacket and set it on the bench between us, and pushed it toward me with two fingers. Gently. The way you push a cup of tea toward a guest.
And I was back in the cold room in the governor’s compound, with the air conditioner roaring like a lion.
“I don’t want your money,” I said.
“It isn’t money.”
Inside was a photograph from an identity card. A white American woman in her thirties, her hair pulled back tight, no smile, eyes that looked at the camera as if it owed her something.
A name, typed. KAYLA ROURKE.
An address in the northwest of the city.
Surveillance, Caravanserai Casino, 2200–0600.

And a gray, smudged copy of a page from something longer, columns of times and capital letters, with a black bar where some words had been hidden. Near the bottom, someone had drawn a red box around one line, and beside it, in a neat small hand, in Dari, had written:
She held the light.

“It’s a page from a log,” the man said. “The record of everything that was seen of your house for forty-one days before the strike. Mostly she watched. She was very thorough. One of the best they had.”
He read me the boxed line, in English first, the way the interpreter had read me a tragic mistake. Then in Dari, with his finger under the words.
Subject on roof. Looks up at aircraft at dawn, daily. Possible awareness of surveillance.
The sun came up over the hotels, and the woman in the gold dress stood and walked away barefoot, carrying her shoes.
“I was looking at my birds,” I said.
“I know. Everybody knows, now. It’s in the report. But she wrote that. And they read it. And after they read it, they decided.”
“And the light?”

“The missile follows a light,” he said. “Someone holds it on the target with their hand. When you turned on the roof to walk to the stairs, she moved the light after you, and it went off you and onto the roof over the room. Over your wife and your daughter.”
I did not say anything.
“She’s here,” he said. “She left the Air Force. She works nights now, in the room behind the cameras at the Caravanserai. She watches the floor all night.” He paused. “She watches you mop it.”
The bus came, late, because it was Tuesday. The doors opened with a sigh. I did not get on.
“Why are you telling me this?”

“Because nobody else will,” he said. “Because the people who decided are in offices you’ll never see, and the officers who signed are retired and playing golf. But she’s real. She’s a woman with an address.” He stood and buttoned his jacket. “I’m not telling you to do anything, Nasim-jan. I want to be very clear about that. I’m only telling you the truth. What a man does with the truth is his own business.”
Then, almost as an afterthought, he set something small on top of the envelope. A flat silver key with an orange plastic tag.

“A locker at the bus station downtown,” he said. “There’s something in it, if you want it. If you don’t, it will go away on its own in a few weeks.” For the first time his eyes did something, a small thing, I could not tell what. “I’m sorry about your family. Truly. I have a daughter too.”
Everybody has a daughter, I thought. Every American I meet has a daughter.
He walked away down the Boulevard, and by the time he reached the corner I had already forgotten his face.

I took the next bus and sat at the back with the envelope on my knees and the key in my fist, watching the city go by. Pawn shops. Wedding chapels with little white steeples and signs that said OPEN 24 HOURS. Palm trees that do not grow here, brought in trucks and watered every day, as if the desert were not a desert.
And I thought about envelopes.

Twice in my life an American has pushed an envelope across to me with two fingers. The first time it was money, in two equal piles, with a paper that said from kindness and not an admission. It said nobody owed me anything.
The second time it was a name.

And I understood, going east on Boulder Highway with the sun in my eyes, that they were two halves of the same envelope. The first said: nobody is responsible. The second said: here is somebody who is.
And both had come to me from a man in an office I would never see, who had a daughter, and who was sorry.
TWENTY-TWO · Kayla
I should tell you I’d been talking to a reporter.

After the Kabul strike, after the seven kids and the water jugs and no one will be punished, I wrote to a woman at a newspaper in New York. Four in the morning, in the break room, no name on it. There was another one. 2019. Maidan Shahr. A man who kept pigeons. I was in the box.
She wrote back in eleven minutes. We’d been talking for months since, on an app that deletes the messages. I told her everything.
The house. The pigeons. The line from day thirty-three, word for word. I’d never forgotten it. I’d written it myself.
You’re the only one who’ll say it was you, she told me. Everybody else says it was the system.
About three weeks after the new porter started, she called me on a Thursday afternoon while I was making Wyatt a sandwich.
“Has anyone from the government contacted you?”
“No. Why?”

“Somebody called my editor. Somebody from the Pentagon, or said they were. They asked if we were working on a 2019 strike in Wardak, with a source who used to be a sensor operator.” She paused. “They used your name, Kayla.”
I stood in the kitchen with the knife in my hand.
“Are you all right?”
“I’m fine,” I said. “I’m making a sandwich.”
After she hung up, I stood at the kitchen window, and the pieces went down next to each other the way they do.
They knew I was talking.

And three weeks ago a man had walked into the Caravanserai and started mopping the floor under my cameras. A man who, out of every city in America, had been sent to mine. Out of every job in mine, sent to that one. To the one place on earth where I would sit in a box all night and watch him.
I’d thought it was the kind of joke the universe makes.
It wasn’t a joke. Somebody had put him there.

I didn’t know why. I want to be clear about that. I only had pieces, and I knew better than anybody alive what happens when you start fitting pieces together and stop asking what they are. But I knew one thing. Somebody was going to tell him who I was, if they hadn’t already.
And I knew the other thing, the thing I’d known since the morning I ate the chicken in the light of the fridge.
I wanted him to.

The next morning, when I got home from my shift, I closed my front door behind me and put my hand on the deadbolt. It’s a good deadbolt. My mother made Gary put it in the week I moved in, because a woman alone with a child in Las Vegas needs a good deadbolt.
And I took my hand away.
I saw him on the bench a few days later.

The bus stop across from my house has a bench under a little metal roof. One morning, when I pulled into my driveway a little after seven, there was a thin man on it in a gray shirt with something stitched in gold over the heart. Not reading. Not on his phone. A bus came and went, and he didn’t get on it.
I didn’t look at him. I walked to my door and went inside. Then I went to the kitchen window and looked at him through the gap in the blinds.
His right shoulder was lower than his left.
He came every morning after that, and every morning I watched him from the kitchen window with my coffee, while Wyatt ate at the counter with his headphones on.
I knew what he was doing. Of course I knew. I’d invented it.

He was learning me. When I came home. Which window was the kitchen. When the kid left for school. He was doing what I’d done to him, with no camera, no satellite, no lag. Just his eyes and a bus bench and all the time in the world. He was patient. He never looked at the house for long, only glanced, like a man checking his watch.
He’d have made a hell of a sensor operator.

Every morning at seven-thirty, Wyatt left for school on his bike, and I stood in the doorway in my uniform and watched him all the way down the street, until he turned the corner by the house with the cactus garden. I’d done it since first grade. My mother said it was overprotective.
That week, I did it differently. I stood in the doorway and watched my son ride away standing on his pedals, his backpack bouncing, and I knew the man on the bench was watching me watch him.
And I thought: look. That’s my son. That’s my little white shape. Look at him ride.
See what I have. See what you could take.

I don’t know why I wanted him to see. Maybe so he’d know it would cost me. Maybe so he’d see I was a mother, and know that I’d understood, every second, what was in the east room. Maybe I wanted to give him a reason. Or a reason not to.
Maybe I just wanted somebody to watch me the way I’d watched him. For once. To be the one on the roof.

A week later, on a Friday, the reporter called again. The same man had called her editor, and this time he wasn’t asking. Classified information. A former service member in violation of her obligations. A serious matter, legally.
“Kayla, I think they’re trying to scare you off. Are they?”
I looked out at the empty bench.
“No,” I said.
And it was true. A man from the Pentagon saying my name should have scared me to death. I had a kid. I had a mortgage. But I wasn’t scared of them.
I was waiting.
That night I called in sick and sat on the couch in the dark with the blinds open a crack. The front door had been unlocked for eight days. Wyatt hadn’t noticed. Kids don’t notice locks.
I don’t own a gun. I spent four thousand hours with my finger on a laser that brought a Hellfire down out of the sky, and I’ve never owned a gun. I don’t like the weight.
I sat there with nothing in my hands, and I thought about how safe I’d been.

That’s the thing nobody understands about the job. You’re safe. Totally. Nobody’s ever going to shoot at you. Nobody’s ever going to come for you. You go home at six and make your kid breakfast. That was the beautiful idea at the heart of it: war without the danger. Killing without the risk. They sold it to us like mercy. Our people come home.

But that’s not war. War is when both sides can die. The man in the balloon in the Civil War could get shot. The boy in the field could get shot. It’s terrible, but it’s fair in a terrible way. Everybody’s under the same sky.
I was never under his sky. He was under mine for forty-one days, and he could never look back and see me, never shoot back, never come.
Until now.

At four in the morning I went to the front door and put my hand on the deadbolt and looked out at the street. The bench was empty. The sky over the mountains was just beginning to change, the way it changed over Maidan Shahr at the start of every shift. The color before light. The color that has no name.
I took my hand off the deadbolt and went back to the couch, and I thought, the way I used to think in the box, like a prayer or a curse:
White means warm. Warm means alive.
Come on, then.
Come and see.
TWENTY-THREE · Nasim
The locker was number 41.

I do not believe in signs. I am a man who fixes radios. But the tag on the key said 41, and when I found the row of gray metal lockers at the back of the bus station downtown, number 41 was at the end, at the height of my eyes, and I stood in front of it a long time before I put the key in.
Inside was a brown paper bag, folded over at the top, the kind you carry your lunch in.
I did not open it there. I did not need to. I had grown up in a country where every man has held one. I knew its weight through the paper the way I knew the weight of a pigeon.
I put it inside my shirt and took the bus home and set it on the shelf beside the empty shoebox.
I did not take it out for days.

I went to work every night and mopped the floor of the Caravanserai, and every night at around three I stopped under the dome by the main aisle and looked up. I looked up the same way as always. The only difference was that now I knew there was a woman behind the black glass, watching me.
Good morning, I thought, at the dome. I am only a porter.
And in the mornings, after my shift, I took two buses northwest across the city to the address on the paper.

It was a small house on a street of small houses all the color of sand, with yards of gray stones where there should have been grass and one small tree each, staked to the ground with wires as if it might try to escape. A white car in the driveway. A basketball hoop with a torn net. A blue child’s bicycle lying on its side on the stones.
Across the street was a bus stop with a bench.
I sat on the bench.
I sat there every morning after that. I told myself I was waiting for the bus. Buses came and went.

I watched her white car turn into the driveway a little after seven, and watched her walk to the door, tired, with a bag over her shoulder, and go in. I watched the kitchen window light up and a shape move past it. At half past seven I watched the door open and a boy come out, nine or ten, thin, with hair that stuck up at the back and a backpack bigger than his body. He picked up the blue bicycle and rode away standing on the pedals, and she stood in the doorway in her uniform and watched him go, until he turned the corner.
Every morning. Until he turned the corner.
I knew what I was doing. I am not a fool. I was learning her day. When the kettle goes on. Where the child sleeps.
This is what she did to me, I thought. Forty-one days.
I could do forty-one days. My young birds did not need me until noon. I had nothing else to do with my mornings.
And I thought: and when I know her day, what then?
On the ninth morning, I opened the bag at my kitchen table, with the curtains closed.

It was what I knew it would be. A small black pistol, new, I think, though I know little of pistols. A box of bullets beside it, unopened. And a piece of paper folded once, with nothing written on it. I turned it over. Nothing. As if someone had meant to write something and decided the paper said enough.
I looked at the pistol for a long time. I did not touch it.
There is something in our law I must tell you now, because it sat at the table with me.

In the old law of our faith, when a man kills another, the family of the dead has a right. It is called qisas [ki-SAAS]. It means retaliation. The same for the same. A life for a life. The family may ask for the death of the one who killed. The law gives them that right. It is not revenge, the way the Americans mean revenge. It is a kind of justice. An old one. Older than Lincoln. Older than Geneva.

But the same law gives the family a second choice. They may forgive, and accept a payment instead of a life. A price for the blood. It is called diya [DEE-ya]. And the Book says that to forgive, and take the diya instead of the life, is better. Closer to God.
And once you take the diya, the qisas is finished. You cannot have both. When you accept the money for the blood, you give up your right to the blood. That is the bargain. The money is the end.
I had taken the money.
Four thousand dollars, in two piles, in a cold room under a picture of the President. I had signed. I had bought grain with it, for my birds.
Not an admission, the paper said. From kindness. They said it was not diya. They said it was a gift, that no one owed me anything.
But I had taken it. And by the law my father knew, the law of every village in Wardak, a man who takes the money for the blood has agreed that the money is enough.
So I argued with myself all morning, the way two old men argue over tea.
You took the diya. The qisas is gone.
It was not diya. They said so themselves. You cannot sell a right they say you never had.
You signed.
I signed so they could close their folder. Not so I could close mine.
And who would you take the life from? The one who held the light? She did not decide. She did not sign. She was a hand at the end of a long arm. Twenty people read that line.
She wrote the line.
She wrote what she saw. You did look up. Every morning. You did.
At my birds.
She did not know they were birds.
She did not look.
Did you look at her? On the bench, this morning? Did you see anything but a woman who watches her son ride to school every morning, until he turns the corner?
I did not answer that one.
I folded the bag closed over the pistol without touching it, put the bag back on the shelf, and I went up to the roof.
The roof of my building is flat and covered in gravel and the big metal boxes that make the cold air. No one ever goes up there but me.

In my first weeks in the city, at a feed store on its edge where people keep horses, I had found an old American with a white beard who kept racing pigeons. He looked at me a long time when I asked, in my bad English, if he sold birds. Then he smiled and said, You’re a pigeon man, and sold me two young pairs for almost nothing, and shook my hand. By the winter they had young of their own.

I had built them a small box on the roof from the wooden crates the vegetables come in at the grocery store. The young ones could not go far yet. They went up in little circles, uncertain, and came down again, and I whistled to them, the two notes and the question, and they were learning it.
That morning I opened the box and let them go.

The first pairs went up, and the young ones after them, over the long low buildings and the parking lots and Boulder Highway, with the mountains all around and the Strip far away to the west, shining in the sun like a row of knives. They turned together. The light caught them. They flashed white, all at once.
I stood with my head back and watched them.
There was no sound in that sky. No high thin buzzing, going around and around.
Only my birds.
And I thought: she is asleep now. In her house the color of sand. With her son at school.
And I thought: I know where she sleeps.
And standing there on the roof in the cold with my face turned up, I did not know which of those two sentences was the one that frightened me.
INTERLUDE FOUR · 2001–2021
A Short History of Watching from Above
The Eye Gets a Hand

This is a true story. It is the story of the machine in this book: where it came from, and how it was armed. It is the last of the four. After this, there is no more history to tell. There are only two people.
The Predator was not built to kill.

In the 1990s the American military wanted a better way to watch. Satellites passed overhead and were gone. Spy planes had pilots, and pilots could be shot down and shown on television. So they built something in between: a long, thin, gray plane with no one in it, a bulge at the front for the cameras and a propeller at the back, that could circle over one place for a whole day and simply look. It flew over the wars in the Balkans. It watched. It did nothing else.
It was a balloon without a man in the basket. A pigeon that would always come home.
Then, in the desert of Nevada, someone asked a question. What if, when it saw something, it could do something about it?

On the twenty-first of February, 2001, on a test range at Nellis Air Force Base outside Las Vegas, a Predator was fitted with a Hellfire, a small fast missile made for helicopters that follows a spot of laser light. On the range below sat an old tank. The Predator fired. The missile followed the light. The tank was destroyed.

It was the first time a Predator, a machine built only to watch, had found a target and destroyed it. From that moment, the thing that watched and the thing that struck were the same machine. Lowe’s balloon and Gavotti’s bomb had become one. The eye in the sky had grown a hand.
That range lies in the desert north of the city, not far from the Strip. Close enough that a man on the roof of a long low building on
Boulder Highway, looking up, would have stood under the same sky.

Seven months later, on the eleventh of September, men flew airliners into buildings in New York and Washington and killed almost three thousand people. Within a month the United States was at war in Afghanistan, and over the city of Kandahar [kan-da-HAAR] an armed Predator fired a missile in war for the first time.

After that there was no going back. The bigger Reaper joined the Predator. They flew over Afghanistan and Iraq, Pakistan, Yemen and Somalia, more and more of them from a base in the desert at Indian Springs that was renamed Creech. The crews drove to work up Highway 95, past the prison and the gas station, and sat in boxes, and watched countries they had never seen. In 2019, the year of the house in Maidan Shahr, American aircraft released more weapons over Afghanistan than in any year since records began: more than seven thousand.
Each one was checked against the rules. Each one had a log. Each one had someone holding a light.
If the eye never has to be seen, who is it answerable to? And what does the man on the roof owe a sky that cannot look back?

When the last plane left Kabul in 2021, the war was over. The drones did not stop. They are flying now, while you read this. Somewhere, right now, someone in a cold box is watching someone else’s morning.
A hundred and sixty years ago, a man in a basket looked down at a boy in a field, and the boy looked up, and each could see the other, and each could die.
Since then, the watcher has become perfectly safe, and the watched perfectly visible, and neither has seen the other’s face.
There is a trailer in the Nevada desert where someone is eating a turkey sandwich with the crusts cut off.
There is a casino called the Caravanserai, a desert inn, a place where strangers are safe for one night, where a man in a gray shirt mops the floor under a black glass dome.
There is a small house the color of sand, with a blue bicycle on the stones and a front door that has not been locked for eight days.
There is a bench across the street.
The history is finished. There is nothing left to tell about balloons or pigeons or bombs or rules.
All that is left is two people, and a door.
V. WHITE HOT
TWENTY-FOUR · Nasim
On the forty-first morning, I counted.

I had told myself I would not. But a man who has kept a shop for twenty years counts everything, and somewhere in the weeks on that bench my mind had begun to keep a tally, the way it keeps the number of screws in a telephone. One morning. Ten. Thirty.
On the forty-first morning I said the number to myself, and I understood what I had done.
Forty-one. The same as hers.
I had watched her for exactly as long as she had watched me.

Weeks had gone by like that, one morning after another, and the forty-first was the coldest of the winter, the kind of cold that comes in the desert after a clear night, the way it came in Maidan Shahr when we kept the mattresses down off the roofs. The mountains to the west were sharp and blue, as if someone had wiped them with a wet cloth.
Her white car turned into the driveway at four minutes past seven.

She walked to the door. She did not look at me. She never looked at me. But I had learned, over forty-one mornings, that she knew I was there. The way you know, on a roof, that someone in the next house is watching you from behind a curtain. Something in the back of the neck.
She put her key in the door and turned it.

The door was not locked. I had known that for weeks. On one of the first mornings I saw her turn the key the wrong way, the unlocking way, and stop, and turn it back. She was pretending. Locking a door that was already open. For me, or for herself, or for her son, I did not know.

At half past seven the boy came out. He had a way of getting on the bicycle that was all his own, a little jump, as if the bicycle might run away if he did not surprise it. A green plastic dinosaur hung from a chain on his backpack, with its mouth open.
He rode away standing on his pedals, and she stood in the doorway and watched him go, all the way, until he turned the corner by the house with the cactus garden.
And then, for the first time in forty-one mornings, she did not go back inside.
She turned her head and looked straight across the street, at the bench, at me.
I have tried to describe that look to myself, in Dari and in my bad English, and I cannot.
It was not angry. It was not afraid. It was not sorry.
It was the look a person gives you across a room when you have both been pretending not to see each other for a long time, at a party, at a funeral, and finally one of you gets tired of pretending.
It lasted perhaps five seconds. She did not wave. She did not nod. She only looked.
Then she went inside and closed the door.
I listened, the way you listen at night for a sound you are afraid of.
I did not hear the lock.
I went home and sat at my kitchen table with the curtains closed, the way I had sat with the pistol, and I took out my telephone.

Months before, in the tent city, Wahid had sent me a picture. A neighbor, a woman, had photographed all the girls in Parisa’s class at the school by the river, on the last day before the winter holidays, because the school had no money for a photographer. Wahid had found it and sent it across the world, and I had looked at it once, in the tent, and closed the telephone.
I looked at it now.

Parisa, in her school uniform, the black dress and the white scarf, in front of a wall painted blue. She was not smiling, because the woman had told the girls to look serious, like ladies, and Parisa was trying very hard to look like a lady. But her mouth was pulled a little to one side, the way it went when she was trying not to laugh. You could see the gap in her teeth. In one more second she would have laughed and ruined it.
You could not see her feet. But I knew what was on them.

That afternoon a young woman with green hair at the pharmacy on the corner showed me how to print it from the machine. A small square of paper came out, warm. It was the first photograph of my daughter I had held since the strike. All the others were under the bricks in the east room.
I put it on the table next to the paper bag and the empty shoebox, and I sat there until it was time to go to work, and I did not decide anything.

I want you to know that. People like to think a man sits at a table and weighs it all, qisas and diya, the old law and the new, and comes to a decision and stands up and goes out the door to do it. It is not like that. I only sat. And the things on the table sat with me. The bag. The box. The girl in front of the blue wall, about to laugh.
That night I mopped the floor of the Caravanserai through the ding and the chime of the thousand machines, the great loft of birds all asking the same question.
At three in the morning I came to the dome by the main aisle, and I stopped under it, and I looked up.

And I did not say good morning in my heart. For the first time, under the black glass, I said something else, out loud, very quietly, in Dari, in case she was there, in case God was listening, in case no one was.
I know you are watching. I know.
Then I pushed my cart away.
I did not know that she was not there. That she had called in sick again that night, and the chair behind my camera was empty.
That she was sitting on a couch in the dark in a house the color of sand, with her door unlocked, waiting for me.
TWENTY-FIVE · Kayla
A stranger came that afternoon, a few hours after I looked at Nasim across the street.

I didn’t hear him. That’s the thing that still gets me. Me, with four thousand hours of listening for the smallest thing. I was in the kitchen making a grocery list, milk, Cheerios, bananas, something hot for dinner, try, and I turned around and there was a man standing in my living room.
He’d come in the front door. Of course he had. I’d left it unlocked.
Not for him. For the other one.
“Ms. Rourke. I’m sorry to startle you. The door was open.”

He was nobody. Gray hair, gray jacket, khakis, brown shoes. The kind of face you’d forget while you were still looking at it. On a casino camera I’d have swung right past him. That’s how you know they’re good.
“I work for an office in Washington,” he said. “Which one doesn’t matter.”

He stood next to the couch where my son plays his video games, with his hands folded like a man at a funeral, and looked around my house. At the Basket of Lonely Socks by the hallway. At Wyatt’s second-grade school picture on the shelf, the one where he’s missing both front teeth.
“Nice kid,” he said.
“Get out of my house.”
“In a minute. I came to help you, Kayla. Just give me a minute.”
He laid it out like a briefing. Calm. One piece next to the last. He’d have been a hell of an intel officer. I think he was one, once.

“You’ve been talking to a reporter about the strike in Wardak. You’ve given her the content of a classified log. That’s a crime. I’m not threatening you. I’m telling you a fact. We’d like it to stop.”
I didn’t say anything.
“The man who mops the floor at the Caravanserai. You know who he is.”
I didn’t have to answer. He watched my face and nodded.
“Of course you do. I read your log, all forty-one days. You knew that man better than his own mother.”
“You put him there,” I said.

“Resettlement is a list. Lists can be edited. Cities, agencies, employers. It’s paperwork.” He looked at Wyatt’s picture again. “You’ve been looking for him since Kabul fell. I’ve seen your search history.”
The back of my neck went cold.
“Why.”

“Because you’re the only one who’ll say it was you,” he said. “Everybody else says it was the system. You say it was a hand. A name. And a story with a name in it runs. A story about a system, nobody reads.” He sighed, like a man tired of his job. “And there’s him. The last living witness to the house. If your reporter finds him, and she will, it isn’t a sensor operator’s guilty conscience anymore. It’s a widower with a broken arm and a picture of his little girl, telling the world what it looked like from the roof. That’s congressional hearings. That’s the whole program on the front page.”
“So what,” I said. “You brought him here so he’d kill me?”
